abdominal part of pectoralis major.kid: This is the lowest strip of your big chest muscle, and it helps you pull your raised arm strongly back down toward your body.
abdominal part of pectoralis major.o: Anterior layer of the rectus sheath (aponeurosis of the external oblique)
abdominal part of pectoralis major.i: Crest of the greater tubercle of the humerus (lateral lip of the intertubercular groove)
abdominal part of pectoralis major.a: Shoulder adduction and internal rotation; pulls the flexed, raised arm downward (extension from a flexed position)
abdominal part of pectoralis major.b: Pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery
abdominal part of pectoralis major.c: The lower fibres are lengthened most when the arm is raised overhead; to stretch, abduct the shoulder to about 135° and then horizontally abduct. Dips and decline bench press emphasise this part.

abductor digiti minimi of foot.kid: It sits along the outer edge of the bottom of your foot and helps your little toe spread outward while holding up the outer arch of your foot.
abductor digiti minimi of foot.o: Medial and lateral processes of the calcaneal tuberosity, plantar aponeurosis
abductor digiti minimi of foot.i: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little toe
abductor digiti minimi of foot.a: Abduction and flexion of the little toe (metatarsophalangeal joint); supports the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot
abductor digiti minimi of foot.c: A first-layer muscle of the sole, palpable along the lateral border of the foot; with pain along the lateral border of the foot, differentiate from problems at the base of the fifth metatarsal.

abductor digiti minimi of hand.kid: It lives in the soft pad on the pinky side of your palm and helps your little finger spread outward, like when you show the number five.
abductor digiti minimi of hand.o: Pisiform, tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris
abductor digiti minimi of hand.i: Ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger and the extensor expansion
abductor digiti minimi of hand.a: Abduction of the little finger (metacarpophalangeal joint); assists flexion of the little finger metacarpophalangeal joint
abductor digiti minimi of hand.n: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
abductor digiti minimi of hand.c: The most superficial muscle of the hypothenar eminence; in ulnar neuropathy (e.g. compression in Guyon's canal) the hypothenar eminence wastes and little finger abduction is weak.

abductor hallucis.kid: It sits along the inner edge of the bottom of your foot, helps your big toe spread outward, and holds up the arch of your foot like a little bridge.
abductor hallucis.o: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity, flexor retinaculum, plantar aponeurosis
abductor hallucis.i: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe (via the medial sesamoid)
abductor hallucis.a: Abduction and flexion of the great toe (metatarsophalangeal joint); supports the medial longitudinal arch of the foot
abductor hallucis.c: Weakness of this muscle is common in flat foot and hallux valgus; the short foot exercise and great toe abduction training can strengthen the arch.

abductor pollicis brevis.kid: It lives in the puffy pad at the bottom of your thumb and helps your thumb lift up away from your palm so you are ready to grab things.
abductor pollicis brevis.o: Flexor retinaculum, tubercle of the scaphoid, tubercle of the trapezium
abductor pollicis brevis.i: Radial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
abductor pollicis brevis.a: Palmar abduction of the thumb (carpometacarpal and metacarpophalangeal joints); assists opposition
abductor pollicis brevis.n: Recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8–T1)
abductor pollicis brevis.b: Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
abductor pollicis brevis.c: In carpal tunnel syndrome, thenar wasting appears first in this muscle; resisted palmar abduction of the thumb is a commonly used test of median nerve motor function.

abductor pollicis longus.kid: It runs from the back of your forearm all the way to the bottom of your thumb and helps your thumb open outward to make a thumbs-up.
abductor pollicis longus.o: Middle part of the posterior surfaces of the ulna and radius, interosseous membrane of the forearm
abductor pollicis longus.i: Radial side of the base of the first metacarpal
abductor pollicis longus.a: Abduction and extension of the thumb (carpometacarpal joint); assists radial deviation of the wrist
abductor pollicis longus.n: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve) (C7–C8)
abductor pollicis longus.c: Shares the first extensor compartment with extensor pollicis brevis, the typical site of de Quervain's tenosynovitis, with a positive Finkelstein test; forms the radial border of the anatomical snuffbox.

acromial part of deltoid.kid: This muscle covers the outside of your shoulder and helps you lift your arm out to the side, like a little bird spreading its wings.
acromial part of deltoid.o: Lateral border of the acromion of the scapula
acromial part of deltoid.a: Shoulder abduction (the main abductor beyond about 15°)
acromial part of deltoid.b: Posterior circumflex humeral artery, deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial artery
acromial part of deltoid.c: Multipennate and powerful; axillary nerve injury (anterior shoulder dislocation, fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus) causes weak abduction and a flattened shoulder contour.

adductor brevis.kid: This short muscle hides on the inside of your thigh and helps you squeeze your spread legs back together.
adductor brevis.o: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
adductor brevis.i: Pectineal line of the femur and proximal part of the medial lip of the linea aspera
adductor brevis.c: Lies deep to adductor longus and pectineus; the anterior and posterior branches of the obturator nerve run in front of and behind it respectively, making it a landmark for identifying the branches of the obturator nerve.

adductor longus.kid: This is the easiest muscle to feel on the inside of your thigh, and it helps you squeeze your legs together, like when you pass a football with the inside of your foot.
adductor longus.o: Anterior surface of the body of the pubis (below the pubic crest)
adductor longus.i: Middle part of the medial lip of the linea aspera of the femur
adductor longus.n: Anterior branch of the obturator nerve (L2–L4)
adductor longus.c: The muscle most often injured in a groin strain; with the hip abducted, a prominent cord-like tendon can be felt beside the pubis. It forms the medial border of the femoral triangle.

adductor magnus.kid: This is the biggest muscle on the inside of your thigh, and it squeezes your legs together and helps push your leg backward when you walk or climb stairs.
adductor magnus.o: Adductor part: inferior pubic ramus, ischial ramus; hamstring part: ischial tuberosity
adductor magnus.i: Adductor part: gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera and medial supracondylar line of the femur; hamstring part: adductor tubercle of the femur
adductor magnus.a: Hip adduction (powerful); adductor part assists hip flexion, hamstring part extends the hip
adductor magnus.n: Adductor part: posterior branch of the obturator nerve (L2–L4); hamstring part: tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L4)
adductor magnus.b: Deep femoral artery and its perforating branches, obturator artery
adductor magnus.c: The adductor hiatus is formed between its two distal insertions, through which the femoral artery and vein enter the popliteal fossa; the adductor tubercle is an important palpation landmark on the medial side of the knee.

adductor minimus.kid: This is the small top piece of the big inner thigh muscle, and it helps squeeze your thigh toward the middle and turn your leg out a tiny bit.
adductor minimus.i: Upper part of the medial lip of the linea aspera of the femur (medial to the gluteal tuberosity)
adductor minimus.a: Hip adduction; assists hip external rotation
adductor minimus.n: Posterior branch of the obturator nerve (L2–L4)
adductor minimus.c: The uppermost part of adductor magnus, with nearly horizontal fibres; usually regarded as part of adductor magnus rather than a separate muscle.

anconeus.kid: This tiny triangle-shaped muscle at the back of your elbow helps straighten your elbow and keeps the elbow joint steady.
anconeus.o: Posterior surface of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
anconeus.i: Lateral surface of the olecranon and proximal posterior surface of the ulna
anconeus.a: Assists triceps brachii in elbow extension; stabilises the elbow joint, slightly abducts the ulna during forearm pronation
anconeus.b: Middle collateral artery (from the deep brachial artery), interosseous recurrent artery
anconeus.c: Lies within the triangle formed by the lateral epicondyle, olecranon and radial head; a surface landmark for elbow joint aspiration and the posterolateral approach to the elbow.

anterior belly of digastric.kid: This little muscle under your chin helps you open your mouth and lifts your throat up when you swallow.
anterior belly of digastric.i: Intermediate tendon (attached by a fibrous pulley to the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone)
anterior belly of digastric.a: Elevates the hyoid bone (swallowing); depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed (mouth opening)
anterior belly of digastric.n: Nerve to mylohyoid (mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, V3)
anterior belly of digastric.c: The anterior belly (V3) and posterior belly (facial nerve) have different innervation; it forms a boundary of the submental and submandibular triangles, and is one of the target muscles of swallowing training (e.g. the Shaker exercise).

aponeurosis of epicranius.kid: This is a tough, thin sheet covering the top of your head that joins the muscles of your forehead and the back of your head together, like a cap.
aponeurosis of epicranius.i: Posteriorly: occipitalis (occipital belly of occipitofrontalis), also attached to the highest nuchal line and external occipital protuberance of the occipital bone
aponeurosis of epicranius.a: Connects frontalis and occipitalis and transmits tension between them, letting the scalp slide forward and backward and assisting raising of the eyebrows
aponeurosis of epicranius.c: The third layer of the scalp; if a scalp laceration cuts transversely through the galea aponeurotica, the wound gapes because of the pull of frontalis and occipitalis. The loose connective tissue beneath it is the "danger area" of the scalp.

ascending part of trapezius.kid: This muscle slants upward in the middle of your back and pulls your shoulder blades down and back so you stand tall instead of slouching.
ascending part of trapezius.o: Spinous processes of T4–T12 and the supraspinous ligament
ascending part of trapezius.i: Medial end of the spine of the scapula (tubercle at the triangular area of the scapular spine)
ascending part of trapezius.a: Depression and retraction of the scapula; upwardly rotates the scapula together with the descending part and serratus anterior
ascending part of trapezius.n: Accessory nerve (CN XI); branches of the cervical plexus (C3–C4) for proprioception
ascending part of trapezius.b: Transverse cervical artery, dorsal scapular artery
ascending part of trapezius.c: Lower trapezius weakness with upper trapezius overactivity is common in shoulder impingement and scapular dyskinesis; the prone Y raise is a commonly used exercise.

brachialis.kid: This muscle hides under your biceps and is the strongest helper for bending your elbow, no matter which way your palm is facing.
brachialis.o: Distal half of the anterior surface of the humerus
brachialis.a: Elbow flexion (the prime elbow flexor, unaffected by forearm pronation or supination)
brachialis.n: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6); a small inferolateral part is supplied by the radial nerve (C7)
brachialis.b: Muscular branches of the brachial artery, radial recurrent artery
brachialis.c: Flexing the elbow with the forearm pronated (reverse curl) relatively emphasises this muscle; a common site of heterotopic ossification (myositis ossificans) after elbow trauma.

brachioradialis.kid: This is the bulgy muscle on the thumb side of your forearm, and it helps you bend your elbow when you lift a cup to drink or swing a hammer.
brachioradialis.o: Proximal two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus, lateral intermuscular septum
brachioradialis.i: Lateral side of the base of the radial styloid process
brachioradialis.a: Elbow flexion (strongest with the forearm in neutral); returns the pronated or supinated forearm to neutral
brachioradialis.c: An elbow flexor despite being supplied by the radial nerve; the brachioradialis reflex tests C5–C6. It stands out clearly on the radial side of the forearm during resisted elbow flexion with the forearm in neutral.

buccinator.kid: This thin muscle inside your cheek works when you blow up a balloon or suck on a straw, and it pushes food back between your teeth when you eat.
buccinator.o: Lateral surfaces of the alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible (molar region), pterygomandibular raphe
buccinator.i: Modiolus at the angle of the mouth, fibres blending into orbicularis oris
buccinator.a: Presses the cheek against the teeth (blowing, sucking); keeps food between the dental arches during chewing
buccinator.n: Buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
buccinator.b: Buccal artery (branch of the maxillary artery), facial artery
buccinator.c: In facial nerve palsy, food collects between the cheek and teeth on the affected side; the parotid duct pierces this muscle and opens opposite the upper second molar.

calcaneal tendon.kid: This is the thick, strong cord just above your heel that carries the power of your calf muscles to your heel so you can stand on tiptoe and jump.
calcaneal tendon.o: Muscle bellies of gastrocnemius and soleus (triceps surae)
calcaneal tendon.i: Posterior surface of the calcaneal tuberosity
calcaneal tendon.a: Transmits the force of triceps surae to the calcaneus, producing ankle plantarflexion; stores and releases elastic energy during running and jumping
calcaneal tendon.c: The thickest and strongest tendon in the body; blood supply is relatively poor 2–6 cm above the insertion, the common site of tendinopathy and rupture. The Thompson test is positive with rupture, and eccentric heel-raise training is a commonly prescribed treatment for tendinopathy.

cervical rotator.kid: These are super tiny muscles hugging the bones of your neck, and they work like little sensors that feel and fine-tune how your neck turns.
cervical rotator.o: Transverse processes (articular processes) of the cervical vertebrae
cervical rotator.i: Lamina and base of the spinous process of the cervical vertebra one to two levels above
cervical rotator.a: Assists cervical extension and rotation to the opposite side; mainly responsible for segmental stability and proprioception
cervical rotator.n: Posterior rami of the cervical nerves
cervical rotator.b: Muscular branches of the deep cervical, vertebral and occipital arteries
cervical rotator.c: The deepest layer of the transversospinalis group, rich in muscle spindles, with a function geared toward postural sensing and segmental control; the cervical rotatores are irregularly developed and often indistinct.

clavicular part of deltoid.kid: This muscle at the front of your shoulder helps you lift your arm forward, like raising your hand to say "I know the answer!"
clavicular part of deltoid.o: Anterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle
clavicular part of deltoid.a: Shoulder flexion, internal rotation and horizontal adduction; assists abduction
clavicular part of deltoid.b: Deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial artery, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries
clavicular part of deltoid.c: The deltopectoral groove lies between it and the clavicular part of pectoralis major and contains the cephalic vein; the anterior fibres are often shortened and tight in people with a rounded-shoulder posture.

clavicular part of pectoralis major.kid: This is the top half of your big chest muscle, near your collarbone, and it helps you lift your arm up in front of you and hug things.
clavicular part of pectoralis major.o: Anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle
clavicular part of pectoralis major.i: Crest of the greater tubercle of the humerus (lateral lip of the intertubercular groove)
clavicular part of pectoralis major.a: Shoulder flexion, horizontal adduction, adduction and internal rotation
clavicular part of pectoralis major.b: Pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery
clavicular part of pectoralis major.c: The incline bench press emphasises this part more; to stretch, abduct the shoulder to about 90° and then horizontally abduct. Palpable below the clavicle, contracting clearly during resisted shoulder flexion.

coccygeus.kid: This small muscle sits deep in your bottom and connects to your tailbone, helping hold up the organs in your tummy like a hammock.
coccygeus.i: Lateral border of the coccyx and of the lower sacrum (S4–S5)
coccygeus.a: Supports the pelvic viscera (posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm); pulls the coccyx forward again after defecation or childbirth
coccygeus.n: Anterior rami of the sacral nerves (S4–S5)
coccygeus.b: Inferior gluteal artery, internal pudendal artery
coccygeus.c: Forms the pelvic diaphragm together with levator ani; can be a source of tenderness in coccydynia or pelvic floor hypertonicity. It lies directly on the pelvic surface of the sacrospinous ligament.

coracobrachialis.kid: This long, thin muscle on the inside of your upper arm helps you lift your arm forward and bring it close to your body, like putting your hand in your pocket.
coracobrachialis.o: Tip of the coracoid process of the scapula (common origin with the short head of biceps brachii)
coracobrachialis.i: Medial surface of the middle of the humeral shaft
coracobrachialis.a: Shoulder flexion and adduction; helps stabilise the humeral head in the glenoid
coracobrachialis.b: Muscular branches of the brachial artery
coracobrachialis.c: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces this muscle and may be compressed when the muscle is hypertrophied or overused; palpable medial to the anterior wall of the axilla with the shoulder abducted and externally rotated.

corrugator supercilii.kid: This little muscle inside your eyebrow squeezes your eyebrows together to make a frown when you are angry or thinking hard.
corrugator supercilii.o: Medial end of the superciliary arch of the frontal bone
corrugator supercilii.i: Skin above the middle of the eyebrow
corrugator supercilii.a: Draws the eyebrow medially and downward, producing vertical wrinkles between the eyebrows (frowning)
corrugator supercilii.n: Temporal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
corrugator supercilii.c: Lies deep to frontalis and orbicularis oculi; the main target muscle for botulinum toxin injection for glabellar lines. Ask the patient to frown when assessing facial nerve function.

deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.kid: This little muscle deep at the bottom of your thumb helps your thumb bend toward your palm so you can pinch things.
deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.i: Radial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb (via the radial sesamoid)
deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.a: Flexion of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint; assists opposition
deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.n: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.b: Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery, branches of the deep palmar arch
deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.c: The superficial head is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve and the deep head mostly by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, so some thumb flexion strength may be preserved after median nerve injury.

deep part of masseter.kid: This is the inner layer of the chewing muscle at the back of your cheek, and it gets hard when you bite down to help you crunch up your food.
deep part of masseter.o: Medial surface of the zygomatic arch and the lower border of its posterior third
deep part of masseter.i: Upper part of the lateral surface of the ramus of the mandible and the coronoid process
deep part of masseter.a: Elevates the mandible (mouth closing, biting); assists retraction of the mandible
deep part of masseter.n: Masseteric nerve (mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, V3)
deep part of masseter.b: Masseteric artery (branch of the maxillary artery)
deep part of masseter.c: The deep fibres are more vertical and more posterior; tenderness and trigger points are common with bruxism, clenching and temporomandibular disorders, and it can be palpated and released with an intraoral–extraoral pincer grip.

depressor anguli oris.kid: This little triangle-shaped muscle below the corner of your mouth pulls the corners down to make a pouty face when you feel sad and want to cry.
depressor anguli oris.o: Oblique line of the mandible (lateral to the mental tubercle)
depressor anguli oris.i: Modiolus and skin at the angle of the mouth
depressor anguli oris.a: Draws the angle of the mouth downward and laterally (expressions of sadness or displeasure)
depressor anguli oris.n: Marginal mandibular branch (and buccal branch) of the facial nerve (CN VII)
depressor anguli oris.b: Inferior labial artery (from the facial artery)
depressor anguli oris.c: Injury to the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (e.g. in submandibular surgery) leaves the angle of the mouth on the affected side unable to be pulled down, so the mouth is asymmetrical when smiling or opening.

depressor labii inferioris.kid: This little muscle under your bottom lip pulls the lip down and out so your bottom teeth show.
depressor labii inferioris.o: Oblique line of the mandible (between the mental symphysis and the mental foramen)
depressor labii inferioris.i: Skin and mucosa of the lower lip, interlacing with orbicularis oris
depressor labii inferioris.a: Draws the lower lip downward and laterally (everts the lower lip, as in expressing doubt or pouting)
depressor labii inferioris.n: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
depressor labii inferioris.b: Inferior labial artery (from the facial artery), mental artery
depressor labii inferioris.c: Its lateral part is covered by depressor anguli oris; in facial palsy rehabilitation it can be facilitated by asking the patient to show the lower teeth.

depressor septi nasi.kid: This little muscle right under your nose pulls the tip of your nose down when you breathe in hard, helping your nostrils open a bit wider.
depressor septi nasi.i: Cartilaginous (mobile) part of the nasal septum and posterior part of the ala of the nose
depressor septi nasi.a: Pulls the nasal septum and tip of the nose downward; assists widening of the nostrils (during deep inspiration)
depressor septi nasi.n: Buccal branch (and zygomatic branch) of the facial nerve (CN VII)
depressor septi nasi.b: Superior labial artery (from the facial artery)
depressor septi nasi.c: Lies deep to orbicularis oris; when this muscle is overactive, the tip of the nose droops noticeably and the upper lip shortens on smiling.

descending part of trapezius.kid: This muscle runs from the back of your head to your shoulder and helps you shrug and carry your backpack, and it gets sore if you look down for too long.
descending part of trapezius.o: Medial third of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone, external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae
descending part of trapezius.i: Posterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle
descending part of trapezius.a: Elevates the shoulder girdle and helps upwardly rotate the scapula; unilateral contraction laterally flexes the neck to the same side and rotates it to the opposite side, bilateral contraction extends the head and neck
descending part of trapezius.n: Accessory nerve (CN XI); branches of the cervical plexus (C3–C4) for proprioception
descending part of trapezius.c: One of the most common sites of myofascial trigger points, which can cause temporal tension-type headache; stretch with contralateral lateral flexion and ipsilateral rotation of the neck plus scapular depression. Accessory nerve injury causes a drooping shoulder and a weak shrug.

diaphragm.kid: This muscle is shaped like a parachute between your chest and your tummy, and when it pulls down, air gets sucked into your lungs, so it is the star of breathing.
diaphragm.o: Sternal part: posterior surface of the xiphoid process; costal part: inner surfaces of the lower six ribs and costal cartilages; lumbar part: bodies of L1–L3 (left and right crura) and the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments
diaphragm.a: Main muscle of inspiration: the dome descends on contraction, enlarging the thoracic cavity; raises intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, defecation, core stability)
diaphragm.n: Phrenic nerve (C3–C5); peripheral sensation from the lower intercostal nerves
diaphragm.b: Pericardiacophrenic, musculophrenic, superior phrenic and inferior phrenic arteries
diaphragm.c: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"; high cervical cord injury affects breathing. Irritation of the diaphragm can refer pain to the shoulder (C4). Abdominal (diaphragmatic) breathing training is fundamental to cardiopulmonary and core rehabilitation.

extensor carpi radialis brevis.kid: This muscle on the back of your forearm helps you tip your wrist up toward the back of your hand and keeps your wrist steady when you make a strong fist.
extensor carpi radialis brevis.o: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
extensor carpi radialis brevis.i: Dorsal surface of the base of the third metacarpal
extensor carpi radialis brevis.a: Wrist extension; assists radial deviation of the wrist, stabilises the wrist during gripping
extensor carpi radialis brevis.n: Deep branch of the radial nerve (C7–C8)
extensor carpi radialis brevis.c: The tendon most often involved in tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis / common extensor tendinopathy); the Cozen test and resisted middle finger extension provoke pain, and eccentric training is commonly prescribed.

extensor carpi radialis longus.kid: This long muscle on the thumb side of your forearm helps you tip your wrist up and tilt it toward your thumb.
extensor carpi radialis longus.o: Distal third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus, lateral intermuscular septum
extensor carpi radialis longus.i: Dorsal surface of the base of the second metacarpal
extensor carpi radialis longus.a: Wrist extension and radial deviation; weakly assists elbow flexion
extensor carpi radialis longus.c: Supplied by the main trunk of the radial nerve (before the deep branch is given off), so wrist extension is still possible in posterior interosseous neuropathy, but the wrist deviates radially as it extends.

extensor digiti minimi.kid: This skinny muscle on the back of your forearm has one special job: straightening your little finger so you can stick your pinky up all by itself.
extensor digiti minimi.o: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
extensor digiti minimi.i: Extensor expansion of the little finger (dorsal digital expansion)
extensor digiti minimi.a: Extension of the little finger (metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints); assists wrist extension
extensor digiti minimi.n: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve) (C7–C8)
extensor digiti minimi.c: Its tendon runs in the fifth extensor compartment (dorsal to the distal radioulnar joint); in rheumatoid arthritis it is one of the first extensor tendons to rupture (Vaughan-Jackson syndrome).

extensor digitorum.kid: This muscle on the back of your forearm splits into four cords going to your fingers and helps you straighten and spread your four fingers together.
extensor digitorum.o: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
extensor digitorum.i: Extensor expansions of digits 2–5, inserting on the dorsal bases of the middle and distal phalanges
extensor digitorum.a: Extension of digits 2–5 (acting mainly at the metacarpophalangeal joints and assisting extension of the interphalangeal joints); assists wrist extension
extensor digitorum.n: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve) (C7–C8)
extensor digitorum.b: Posterior interosseous artery, interosseous recurrent artery
extensor digitorum.c: Rupture of the distal insertion causes mallet finger, and rupture of the central slip causes a boutonnière deformity; intertendinous connections between the tendons on the back of the hand limit independent extension of each finger.

extensor digitorum brevis.kid: This small, soft lump of muscle on the outer top of your foot helps your middle toes lift up.
extensor digitorum brevis.o: Superolateral surface of the calcaneus (anterior to the sinus tarsi), inferior extensor retinaculum
extensor digitorum brevis.i: Lateral sides of the extensor digitorum longus tendons to toes 2–4 (dorsal digital expansion)
extensor digitorum brevis.a: Assists extension of toes 2–4 (metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints)
extensor digitorum brevis.b: Dorsalis pedis artery, lateral tarsal artery
extensor digitorum brevis.c: The soft bulge on the dorsum of the foot in front of the lateral malleolus is this muscle belly, easily mistaken for swelling after an ankle sprain; its wasting can be a sign of L5 nerve root or deep fibular nerve pathology.

extensor digitorum longus.kid: This long muscle on the outer front of your lower leg lifts your four smaller toes up and raises the front of your foot when you walk so you do not trip.
extensor digitorum longus.o: Lateral condyle of the tibia, upper three-quarters of the anterior surface of the fibula, interosseous membrane of the leg
extensor digitorum longus.i: Dorsal bases of the middle and distal phalanges of toes 2–5 (via the dorsal digital expansion)
extensor digitorum longus.c: Also weak in foot drop caused by deep fibular nerve or L5 injury; when tibialis anterior is weak it compensates for dorsiflexion, which over time can lead to claw toes.

extensor hallucis brevis.kid: This little muscle on the top of your foot has one special job: lifting your big toe up.
extensor hallucis brevis.o: Superolateral surface of the calcaneus (anterior to the sinus tarsi), inferior extensor retinaculum
extensor hallucis brevis.i: Dorsal surface of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe
extensor hallucis brevis.a: Extension of the great toe metatarsophalangeal joint
extensor hallucis brevis.c: The most medial slip of extensor digitorum brevis, often regarded as part of the same muscle; its tendon crosses obliquely over the dorsalis pedis artery on the dorsum of the foot and is a guide to finding that artery.

extensor hallucis longus.kid: This muscle runs from the front of your lower leg to your big toe, and it lifts your big toe up strongly and helps pull your foot up too.
extensor hallucis longus.o: Middle part of the anterior surface of the fibula, interosseous membrane of the leg
extensor hallucis longus.i: Dorsal surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe
extensor hallucis longus.a: Extension of the great toe (metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints); ankle dorsiflexion
extensor hallucis longus.c: Resisted extension of the great toe is the key muscle test for the L5 nerve root; the dorsalis pedis pulse can be felt lateral to its tendon at the front of the ankle.

extensor indicis.kid: This little muscle deep in your forearm lets your pointer finger straighten all by itself, so it is what you use to point at things.
extensor indicis.o: Distal third of the posterior surface of the ulna, interosseous membrane of the forearm
extensor indicis.i: Extensor expansion of the index finger (on the ulnar side of the extensor digitorum tendon to the index finger)
extensor indicis.a: Independent extension of the index finger (metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints); assists wrist extension
extensor indicis.n: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve) (C7–C8)
extensor indicis.c: Shares the fourth extensor compartment with extensor digitorum; because it can be sacrificed on its own, it is often used as a donor tendon for tendon transfer (e.g. reconstruction of a ruptured extensor pollicis longus).

extensor pollicis brevis.kid: This little muscle runs from the back of your forearm to your thumb and helps straighten the bottom part of your thumb, like when you give a thumbs-up.
extensor pollicis brevis.o: Distal third of the posterior surface of the radius, interosseous membrane of the forearm
extensor pollicis brevis.i: Dorsal surface of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
extensor pollicis brevis.a: Extension of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint; assists extension and abduction of the thumb carpometacarpal joint
extensor pollicis brevis.n: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve) (C7–C8)
extensor pollicis brevis.c: Shares the first extensor compartment with abductor pollicis longus and is one of the tendons involved in de Quervain's tenosynovitis; forms the radial border of the anatomical snuffbox.

extensor pollicis longus.kid: This muscle runs from the back of your forearm to the tip of your thumb and helps your whole thumb straighten and tip backward, like a hitchhiker's thumb.
extensor pollicis longus.o: Middle third of the posterior surface of the ulna, interosseous membrane of the forearm
extensor pollicis longus.i: Dorsal surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
extensor pollicis longus.a: Extension of the thumb interphalangeal joint, and extension of the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints; assists thumb adduction and retroposition
extensor pollicis longus.n: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve) (C7–C8)
extensor pollicis longus.c: Its tendon changes direction around the dorsal tubercle of the radius (Lister's tubercle) and may fray and rupture after a distal radius fracture or in rheumatoid arthritis; forms the ulnar border of the anatomical snuffbox.

external anal sphincter.kid: This ring of muscle around the opening of your bottom squeezes tight like a rubber band so you can hold your poo until you get to the toilet.
external anal sphincter.o: Perineal body (central tendon of the perineum) and perianal skin
external anal sphincter.i: Anococcygeal ligament (attached to the tip of the coccyx)
external anal sphincter.a: Voluntary contraction closes the anal canal and maintains faecal continence; keeps a resting tonic contraction
external anal sphincter.n: Inferior rectal nerve from the pudendal nerve (S2–S4)
external anal sphincter.b: Inferior rectal artery (branch of the internal pudendal artery)
external anal sphincter.c: Divided into subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts, the deep part being continuous with puborectalis; obstetric injury or pudendal neuropathy can cause faecal incontinence, which can be treated with pelvic floor muscle training and biofeedback.

external intercostal muscle.kid: These muscles sit between your ribs and lift the ribs up when you breathe in, making your chest bigger to hold more air.
external intercostal muscle.o: Lower border of the rib above
external intercostal muscle.i: Upper border of the rib below (fibres run obliquely forward and downward)
external intercostal muscle.a: Elevates the ribs and expands the thoracic cage during inspiration; maintains tension of the intercostal spaces, preventing them from being drawn in or bulging out during breathing
external intercostal muscle.b: Posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal arteries (branches of the internal thoracic and musculophrenic arteries)
external intercostal muscle.c: Fibres run forward and downward like "hands in pockets"; anteriorly, near the sternum, it is replaced by the external intercostal membrane. The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs along the lower border of the rib, so the needle in thoracentesis should be inserted along the upper border of the rib.

external oblique.kid: This is the outermost muscle on the sides of your tummy, and it helps you bend forward, twist and lean sideways, and it squeezes your tummy tight when you cough.
external oblique.o: External surfaces of ribs 5–12 (interdigitating with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi)
external oblique.i: Linea alba, pubic tubercle, outer lip of the anterior half of the iliac crest; the lower border of the aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament
external oblique.a: Bilateral: trunk flexion, raises intra-abdominal pressure, assists forced expiration; unilateral: lateral flexion of the trunk to the same side, rotation to the opposite side
external oblique.b: Lower posterior intercostal arteries, subcostal artery, deep circumflex iliac artery
external oblique.c: Fibres run forward and downward (hands in pockets); the right external oblique works with the left internal oblique to rotate the trunk to the left. The superficial inguinal ring in its aponeurosis is the exit point for inguinal hernias.

fibularis brevis.kid: This muscle on the lower outside of your leg turns the sole of your foot outward and protects your ankle from twisting when you walk on bumpy ground.
fibularis brevis.o: Distal two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula
fibularis brevis.i: Tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal (lateral side of the base)
fibularis brevis.a: Eversion of the foot; assists ankle plantarflexion
fibularis brevis.b: Fibular artery, branches of the anterior tibial artery
fibularis brevis.c: An inversion ankle sprain can cause an avulsion fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal; the tendon is prone to longitudinal tears or subluxation behind the lateral malleolus. A focus of eversion strength training after ankle sprain.

fibularis longus.kid: This long muscle on the outside of your lower leg has a cord that wraps under your foot, turning your sole outward and holding up the arch of your foot.
fibularis longus.o: Head of the fibula, proximal two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula
fibularis longus.i: Medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal (lateral side of the plantar surface)
fibularis longus.a: Eversion of the foot, ankle plantarflexion; depresses the first metatarsal, supports the transverse arch and lateral longitudinal arch of the foot
fibularis longus.b: Fibular artery, branches of the anterior tibial artery
fibularis longus.c: Its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and then through the groove of the cuboid to cross the sole obliquely; the common fibular nerve lies deep to this muscle as it winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is vulnerable to compression. Reaction time of this muscle is often delayed in chronic ankle instability.

fibularis tertius.kid: This little muscle at the lower front of your leg helps pull your foot up and turns the sole outward a little at the same time.
fibularis tertius.o: Distal third of the anterior surface of the fibula, interosseous membrane of the leg
fibularis tertius.i: Dorsal surface of the base of the fifth metatarsal
fibularis tertius.a: Ankle dorsiflexion; eversion of the foot
fibularis tertius.c: Really a part split off from extensor digitorum longus, belonging to the anterior compartment (not the lateral compartment); absent in some people. Helps lift the lateral border of the foot during swing phase.

first lumbrical of foot.kid: This skinny muscle in the bottom of your foot looks like a little worm, and it bends the base of your second toe while keeping its tip straight so your foot grips the ground well.
first lumbrical of foot.o: Medial border of the flexor digitorum longus tendon to the second toe
first lumbrical of foot.i: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the second toe and the dorsal digital expansion (extensor expansion)
first lumbrical of foot.a: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint of the second toe while extending the interphalangeal joints
first lumbrical of foot.c: A second-layer muscle of the sole; the first lumbrical is supplied by the medial plantar nerve and the other three by the lateral plantar nerve. Weakness of the intrinsic foot muscles is associated with claw toes and hammer toes.

first plantar interosseous of foot.kid: This little muscle hides between the bones of your foot and helps your third toe move toward your second toe, bringing your toes together.
first plantar interosseous of foot.o: Base and medial surface of the third metatarsal
first plantar interosseous of foot.i: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the third toe and the dorsal digital expansion
first plantar interosseous of foot.a: Adduction of the third toe (toward the second toe); flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint, assists extension of the interphalangeal joints
first plantar interosseous of foot.n: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
first plantar interosseous of foot.b: Plantar arterial arch, plantar metatarsal arteries
first plantar interosseous of foot.c: A fourth-layer (deepest) muscle of the sole; the axis for adduction and abduction in the foot is the second toe (the middle finger in the hand). Plantar interossei adduct (PAD), dorsal interossei abduct (DAB).

flexor accessorius.kid: This square muscle in the middle of the bottom of your foot tugs on the long cord that bends your toes so they can curl straight down.
flexor accessorius.o: Medial border (medial head) and lateral border (lateral head) of the plantar surface of the calcaneus
flexor accessorius.i: Posterolateral border of the flexor digitorum longus tendon
flexor accessorius.a: Assists flexion of toes 2–5; corrects the oblique pull of the flexor digitorum longus tendon so the toes flex along their long axis
flexor accessorius.b: Lateral plantar artery, medial plantar artery
flexor accessorius.c: Also known as quadratus plantae, a second-layer muscle of the sole; with pain on the plantar surface of the calcaneus, differentiate from plantar fasciitis. It can still assist toe flexion when the ankle is plantarflexed.

flexor carpi radialis.kid: This muscle on the inside of your forearm helps you bend your wrist toward your palm and tilt it toward your thumb, like when you throw a ball.
flexor carpi radialis.o: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
flexor carpi radialis.i: Palmar surface of the base of the second metacarpal (some fibres to the base of the third metacarpal)
flexor carpi radialis.a: Wrist flexion and radial deviation; weakly assists forearm pronation and elbow flexion
flexor carpi radialis.b: Branches of the ulnar artery (ulnar recurrent artery), radial artery
flexor carpi radialis.c: Its tendon is prominent at the wrist, and the radial pulse is palpated just on its radial side; the median nerve lies deep in the interval between it and the palmaris longus tendon. Part of the flexor–pronator group associated with golfer's elbow.

flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot.kid: This little muscle on the outer side of the bottom of your foot helps bend the base of your little toe downward to grip the ground.
flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot.o: Plantar surface of the base of the fifth metatarsal, sheath of the fibularis longus tendon
flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot.i: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little toe
flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot.a: Flexion of the little toe metatarsophalangeal joint
flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot.n: Superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot.c: A third-layer muscle of the sole, lying medial and deep to abductor digiti minimi; palpable along the plantar surface of the fifth metatarsal.

flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand.kid: This little muscle on the pinky side of your palm helps your little finger bend from its base toward your palm and gives it power when you hold things.
flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand.o: Hook of the hamate, flexor retinaculum
flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand.i: Ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger
flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand.a: Flexion of the little finger metacarpophalangeal joint
flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand.n: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand.c: Lies on the radial side of abductor digiti minimi; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and the deep branch of the ulnar artery pass between the origins of the two muscles. A fracture of the hook of the hamate can affect the nerve here.

flexor digitorum brevis.kid: This muscle right in the middle of the bottom of your foot helps your four smaller toes curl down to grip the ground and also helps hold up your arch.
flexor digitorum brevis.o: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity, plantar aponeurosis
flexor digitorum brevis.i: Both sides of the middle phalanges of toes 2–5 (each tendon splits to let the flexor digitorum longus tendon pass through)
flexor digitorum brevis.a: Flexion of the proximal interphalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints of toes 2–5; supports the longitudinal arch of the foot
flexor digitorum brevis.b: Medial plantar artery, lateral plantar artery
flexor digitorum brevis.c: A first-layer muscle of the sole lying directly deep to the plantar aponeurosis, equivalent to flexor digitorum superficialis in the hand; it can be trained with towel curls and marble pick-ups, and is often tight in plantar fasciitis.

flexor digitorum longus.kid: This muscle deep in the back of your lower leg has cords that go around the inside of your ankle to the bottom of your foot, helping the tips of your four smaller toes curl down hard to grip the ground.
flexor digitorum longus.o: Middle part of the posterior surface of the tibia (below the soleal line)
flexor digitorum longus.i: Plantar surface of the bases of the distal phalanges of toes 2–5
flexor digitorum longus.a: Flexion of toes 2–5 (mainly the distal interphalangeal joints); assists ankle plantarflexion and foot inversion, supports the longitudinal arch of the foot
flexor digitorum longus.c: Its tendon passes through the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus (the Dick in Tom, Dick and Harry); it is often used as the transfer tendon in reconstruction for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, and is also associated with medial tibial stress syndrome.

flexor digitorum profundus.kid: It hides deep in your forearm and bends your fingertips so you can hold things tight.
flexor digitorum profundus.o: Upper 3/4 of the anterior and medial surfaces of the ulna; interosseous membrane of the forearm
flexor digitorum profundus.i: Palmar surface of the bases of the distal phalanges of digits 2–5
flexor digitorum profundus.a: Flexes the distal interphalangeal joints of digits 2–5; assists flexion of the proximal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal joints and wrist
flexor digitorum profundus.n: Radial half (digits 2 and 3): anterior interosseous nerve (branch of the median nerve, C8–T1); ulnar half (digits 4 and 5): ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
flexor digitorum profundus.c: Stabilise the middle phalanx and ask the patient to bend the fingertip to test this muscle in isolation; avulsion of the tendon from the distal phalanx is called jersey finger and most often affects the ring finger.

flexor hallucis longus.kid: It runs from your lower leg all the way to your big toe and helps the big toe push down on the ground when you walk or stand on tiptoe.
flexor hallucis longus.o: Lower 2/3 of the posterior surface of the fibula; lower part of the interosseous membrane of the leg
flexor hallucis longus.i: Plantar surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe
flexor hallucis longus.a: Flexes all joints of the great toe; assists ankle plantarflexion and foot inversion, and supports the medial longitudinal arch
flexor hallucis longus.c: The tendon curves behind the talus and beneath the sustentaculum tali; repeated rising onto the toes makes ballet dancers prone to tendinitis (dancer's tendinitis), with snapping or pain behind the medial malleolus.

flexor pollicis longus.kid: It bends the tip of your thumb so you can pinch a pencil and other little things.
flexor pollicis longus.o: Middle part of the anterior surface of the radius; adjacent interosseous membrane of the forearm
flexor pollicis longus.i: Palmar surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
flexor pollicis longus.a: Flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb; assists flexion of the thumb metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints
flexor pollicis longus.n: Anterior interosseous nerve (branch of the median nerve, C8–T1)
flexor pollicis longus.c: In anterior interosseous nerve lesions the thumb tip cannot flex, so the patient cannot make a round OK sign (it becomes a flat pinch).

flexor retinaculum of wrist.kid: It is like a strong strap across your wrist that keeps the finger-bending cords in their tunnel so they do not slip around.
flexor retinaculum of wrist.o: Ulnar side: pisiform, hook of the hamate
flexor retinaculum of wrist.i: Radial side: tubercle of the scaphoid, tubercle of the trapezium
flexor retinaculum of wrist.a: Spans the carpal groove to form the roof of the carpal tunnel; holds the finger flexor tendons in place to prevent bowstringing, and serves as an origin for the thenar and hypothenar muscles
flexor retinaculum of wrist.c: Compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel beneath it is carpal tunnel syndrome; Phalen's test and Tinel's sign are the common examinations, and severe cases are decompressed by surgically dividing this ligament.

fourth lumbrical of foot.kid: It is a little worm-shaped muscle in the sole of your foot that helps your little toe lie flat on the ground instead of curling up.
fourth lumbrical of foot.o: Adjacent sides of the flexor digitorum longus tendons to the 4th and 5th toes
fourth lumbrical of foot.i: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th toe and the extensor expansion
fourth lumbrical of foot.a: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint of the 5th toe while extending the interphalangeal joints
fourth lumbrical of foot.n: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
fourth lumbrical of foot.b: Lateral plantar artery, plantar metatarsal arteries
fourth lumbrical of foot.c: Weakness of the intrinsic foot muscles predisposes to claw toes; the short foot exercise and towel curls train the intrinsic foot muscles.

frontalis.kid: It sits on your forehead and lifts your eyebrows and wrinkles your forehead when you are surprised.
frontalis.i: Skin of the eyebrows and forehead, interlacing with fibres of orbicularis oculi and corrugator supercilii
frontalis.a: Raises the eyebrows and produces horizontal wrinkles of the forehead
frontalis.n: Temporal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
frontalis.b: Supraorbital artery, supratrochlear artery, superficial temporal artery
frontalis.c: In peripheral facial nerve palsy (e.g. Bell's palsy) the affected side cannot raise the eyebrow or wrinkle the forehead; in central lesions frontalis function is spared, which helps distinguish the two.

gemellus inferior.kid: It is a small muscle deep in your bottom that helps turn your thigh outward and keeps your hip joint steady.
gemellus inferior.o: Upper part of the ischial tuberosity
gemellus inferior.i: Blends with the obturator internus tendon to insert on the medial surface of the greater trochanter of the femur
gemellus inferior.a: External rotation of the hip; assists abduction when the hip is flexed, and stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
gemellus inferior.b: Medial circumflex femoral artery, inferior gluteal artery
gemellus inferior.c: Together with the superior gemellus and obturator internus it forms the triceps coxae; it belongs to the deep external rotators of the hip and is an important dynamic stabiliser of the hip joint.

gemellus superior.kid: It hides deep in your bottom and works with its little neighbours to turn your thigh outward and steady your hip.
gemellus superior.o: Outer surface of the ischial spine
gemellus superior.i: Blends with the obturator internus tendon to insert on the medial surface of the greater trochanter of the femur
gemellus superior.a: External rotation of the hip; assists abduction when the hip is flexed, and stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
gemellus superior.b: Inferior gluteal artery, internal pudendal artery
gemellus superior.c: Lies below piriformis, with the sciatic nerve passing behind it; in the posterior approach to the hip this group of short external rotators often has to be divided and then repaired.

geniohyoid.kid: It sits inside your chin and pulls the little bone above your throat forward and up when you swallow.
geniohyoid.o: Inferior mental spine on the inner surface of the mandible
geniohyoid.i: Anterior surface of the body of the hyoid bone
geniohyoid.a: Pulls the hyoid bone forward and upward and shortens the floor of the mouth (swallowing); with the hyoid fixed, assists depression of the mandible (mouth opening)
geniohyoid.n: Fibres of the first cervical nerve (C1) travelling with the hypoglossal nerve
geniohyoid.b: Sublingual branch of the lingual artery
geniohyoid.c: A suprahyoid muscle and the main muscle moving the hyoid forward during swallowing; swallowing exercises such as the Shaker head-lift exercise target this muscle group.

gluteus maximus.kid: It is the biggest, strongest muscle in your bottom and helps you stand up, climb stairs, run and jump.
gluteus maximus.o: Ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, dorsal surface of the sacrum and coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament, thoracolumbar fascia
gluteus maximus.i: Iliotibial tract (most fibres), gluteal tuberosity of the femur
gluteus maximus.a: Hip extension and external rotation; upper fibres assist abduction, lower fibres assist adduction; helps stabilise the extended knee through the iliotibial tract
gluteus maximus.b: Inferior gluteal artery, superior gluteal artery
gluteus maximus.c: Most active during sit-to-stand, stair climbing and running; weakness produces a gluteus maximus gait (backward trunk lean). Bridges, squats and hip thrusts are common training exercises.

gluteus medius.kid: It sits on the side of your bottom and keeps your hips level when you stand on one foot so you do not tip over.
gluteus medius.o: Outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines
gluteus medius.i: Lateral surface of the greater trochanter of the femur
gluteus medius.a: Hip abduction; anterior fibres internally rotate and assist hip flexion, posterior fibres externally rotate and assist hip extension; stabilises the pelvis in single-leg stance
gluteus medius.c: Weakness produces a Trendelenburg sign (drop of the opposite side of the pelvis) or a compensatory lateral trunk lean; side-lying leg raises, clamshells and lateral band walks are common training exercises.

gluteus minimus.kid: It is the small innermost muscle of your bottom that helps lift your leg out to the side and keeps your hips steady when you walk.
gluteus minimus.o: Outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines
gluteus minimus.i: Anterior surface of the greater trochanter of the femur
gluteus minimus.a: Hip abduction and internal rotation; in single-leg stance stabilises the pelvis and holds the femoral head firmly in the acetabulum
gluteus minimus.c: Along with gluteus medius tendinopathy, a common cause of greater trochanteric pain syndrome; trigger points can refer pain to the lateral thigh and lower leg, mimicking sciatica.

gracilis.kid: It is a long, thin muscle on the inside of your thigh that helps you squeeze your legs together and bend your knee.
gracilis.o: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
gracilis.i: Medial surface of the upper tibia (pes anserinus)
gracilis.a: Hip adduction; knee flexion, and assists internal rotation of the leg when the knee is flexed
gracilis.b: Obturator artery, medial circumflex femoral artery
gracilis.c: Forms the pes anserinus together with sartorius and semitendinosus, where pes anserine bursitis can occur; its tendon is often harvested with the semitendinosus tendon as a graft for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris.kid: It is on the little-finger side of your forearm and helps tip your wrist back and wave your hand toward your little finger.
humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris.o: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris.i: Ulnar side of the dorsal surface of the base of the 5th metacarpal
humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris.a: Wrist extension and ulnar deviation (adduction); stabilises the wrist when making a fist
humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris.n: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve, C7–C8)
humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris.c: The tendon runs in a groove on the dorsal side of the ulnar head; tennis players and golfers can develop tendinitis or subluxation, causing ulnar-sided wrist pain.

humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris.kid: It is on the little-finger side of your forearm and helps bend your wrist toward your palm and wave your hand toward your little finger.
humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris.o: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris.i: Pisiform, and via the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments to the hook of the hamate and the base of the 5th metacarpal
humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris.b: Ulnar artery, posterior ulnar recurrent artery
humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris.c: The ulnar nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads (cubital tunnel), a common site of ulnar nerve compression; the tendon is easily palpated just proximal to the pisiform.

humeral head of pronator teres.kid: It helps you turn your palm to face down, like turning a doorknob or pouring water out of a cup.
humeral head of pronator teres.o: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon) and the lower part of the medial supracondylar ridge
humeral head of pronator teres.i: Middle of the lateral surface of the radius (pronator tuberosity)
humeral head of pronator teres.b: Branches of the ulnar and radial arteries
humeral head of pronator teres.c: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads; compression here is called pronator teres syndrome, and resisted pronation can provoke proximal forearm pain and numbness in the hand.

humeroulnar head of flexor digitorum sup.kid: It bends the middle joints of your fingers, which you need for making a fist and grabbing things.
humeroulnar head of flexor digitorum sup.o: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon), ulnar collateral ligament, medial border of the coronoid process of the ulna
humeroulnar head of flexor digitorum sup.i: Both sides of the shafts of the middle phalanges of digits 2–5
humeroulnar head of flexor digitorum sup.a: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of digits 2–5; assists flexion of the metacarpophalangeal joints and wrist
humeroulnar head of flexor digitorum sup.c: Hold the other fingers in extension and ask the patient to flex the finger to test flexor digitorum superficialis in isolation; the median nerve passes beneath the tendinous arch between the humeroulnar and radial heads.

iliacus.kid: It lies like a fan on the inside of your hip bone and helps lift your thigh up for walking and kicking a ball.
iliacus.o: Upper 2/3 of the iliac fossa, inner lip of the iliac crest, ala of the sacrum and anterior sacroiliac ligament
iliacus.i: Joins the psoas major tendon to insert on the lesser trochanter of the femur and just below it
iliacus.a: Hip flexion; with the lower limb fixed, tilts the pelvis anteriorly and assists sitting up from supine
iliacus.b: Iliac branch of the iliolumbar artery
iliacus.c: Together with psoas major it forms iliopsoas, the strongest hip flexor; tightness gives a positive Thomas test and increases lumbar lordosis, and it can be stretched in a lunge position.

iliococcygeus.kid: It is a hammock-like muscle at the bottom of your pelvis that holds up the organs in your tummy from below.
iliococcygeus.o: Tendinous arch of levator ani (thickening of the obturator internus fascia), ischial spine
iliococcygeus.a: Supports the pelvic viscera, elevates the pelvic floor and resists increases in intra-abdominal pressure
iliococcygeus.n: Nerve to levator ani (S3–S4), partly from branches of the pudendal nerve
iliococcygeus.b: Inferior gluteal artery, internal pudendal artery
iliococcygeus.c: The posterolateral part of levator ani; childbirth or chronically raised abdominal pressure can injure it, leading to pelvic organ prolapse, and Kegel exercises are the basic training.

iliocostalis cervicis.kid: It runs from your upper ribs to your neck and helps you tip your neck back or lean it to the side.
iliocostalis cervicis.i: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C4–C6
iliocostalis cervicis.a: Bilateral contraction extends the cervical spine; unilateral contraction side-bends the neck to the same side
iliocostalis cervicis.n: Posterior rami of the lower cervical and upper thoracic spinal nerves
iliocostalis cervicis.b: Deep cervical artery, dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
iliocostalis cervicis.c: The cervical part of the most lateral column of erector spinae; prolonged forward head posture tends to overload the extensors at the cervicothoracic junction and make them ache.

iliocostalis lumborum.kid: It sits on both sides of your lower back and helps you stand up straight and bend to the side.
iliocostalis lumborum.o: Common tendon of erector spinae: posterior iliac crest, dorsal surface of the sacrum, lumbar spinous processes and thoracolumbar fascia
iliocostalis lumborum.a: Bilateral contraction extends the spine; unilateral contraction side-bends the trunk to the same side; eccentrically controls trunk flexion when bending forward
iliocostalis lumborum.n: Lateral branches of the posterior rami of the spinal nerves
iliocostalis lumborum.b: Lumbar arteries, dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
iliocostalis lumborum.c: A common site of tightness and tenderness in low back pain; in full trunk flexion the electrical activity of erector spinae falls silent (flexion-relaxation phenomenon), which is often absent in people with chronic low back pain.

iliocostalis thoracis.kid: It runs up along the ribs in your back and helps you keep your back straight instead of slouching.
iliocostalis thoracis.o: Angles of the lower 6 ribs (medial to the insertion of iliocostalis lumborum)
iliocostalis thoracis.i: Angles of the upper 6 ribs and the transverse process of C7
iliocostalis thoracis.a: Bilateral contraction extends the thoracic spine; unilateral contraction side-bends the trunk to the same side
iliocostalis thoracis.n: Lateral branches of the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves
iliocostalis thoracis.b: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
iliocostalis thoracis.c: The thoracic part of the most lateral column of erector spinae, maintaining upright thoracic posture; in a hunched posture it is chronically lengthened and weak, and can be trained with prone extension exercises.

iliotibial tract.kid: It is a long, strong band down the outside of your thigh, from your hip to just below your knee, that helps your leg stand steady.
iliotibial tract.o: Tubercle of the iliac crest, receiving fibres from tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus
iliotibial tract.i: Gerdy's tubercle on the lateral condyle of the tibia
iliotibial tract.a: Thickened lateral band of the fascia lata; transmits the force of tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus, stabilising the lateral hip and the lateral side of the extended knee
iliotibial tract.c: Iliotibial band syndrome is a common cause of lateral knee pain in runners, most painful over the lateral femoral epicondyle at about 30 degrees of knee flexion; tightness is assessed with Ober's test, and treatment focuses on strengthening the hip abductors.

inferior oblique part of longus colli.kid: It lies on the front of your neck bones and helps you nod your head down and hold your head up steadily.
inferior oblique part of longus colli.o: Anterior surfaces of the bodies of T1–T3
inferior oblique part of longus colli.i: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C5–C6
inferior oblique part of longus colli.a: Flexes the cervical spine; unilateral contraction assists side-bending of the neck and rotation to the opposite side; stabilises the cervical lordosis
inferior oblique part of longus colli.n: Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C2–C6)
inferior oblique part of longus colli.b: Branches of the inferior thyroid, ascending cervical and vertebral arteries
inferior oblique part of longus colli.c: A deep neck flexor that is often inhibited and weak after whiplash injury and in chronic neck pain; assess with the craniocervical flexion test (pressure biofeedback unit) and train with chin tucks.

infraspinatus muscle.kid: It lies on the back of your shoulder blade and helps turn your arm outward, like pulling your hand back before throwing a ball.
infraspinatus muscle.i: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus
infraspinatus muscle.a: External rotation of the shoulder; stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid fossa (rotator cuff)
infraspinatus muscle.c: One of the rotator cuff muscles; test with resisted external rotation with the arm at the side and the elbow flexed to 90 degrees. Compression of the suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch causes isolated atrophy of this muscle, commonly seen in volleyball players.

inguinal ligament.kid: It is a band where your tummy meets your thigh, like a rope stretched from the outer hip bone to the middle at the front.
inguinal ligament.a: Formed by the thickened, rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis; forms the floor of the inguinal canal, with iliopsoas, the femoral nerve and the femoral vessels passing beneath it
inguinal ligament.c: An important surface landmark: the femoral pulse lies below the midpoint of the ligament; inguinal hernias protrude above the ligament, whereas femoral hernias protrude below it.

innermost intercostal muscle.kid: It is the thin innermost layer of muscle between your ribs that helps pull the ribs down when you blow out hard.
innermost intercostal muscle.o: Lower border of the rib above (inner side of the costal groove)
innermost intercostal muscle.i: Upper border of the rib below
innermost intercostal muscle.a: Acts with the internal intercostals to depress the ribs in forced expiration; maintains tension of the intercostal spaces
innermost intercostal muscle.b: Posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal arteries
innermost intercostal muscle.c: The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles in the costal groove, so the needle for thoracentesis should be inserted along the upper border of the rib.

intermediate tendon.kid: It is a short cord under your chin that joins the front and back parts of a two-part muscle and hangs them from the little bone in your throat.
intermediate tendon.o: Posterior belly of digastric (arising from the mastoid notch of the temporal bone)
intermediate tendon.i: Anterior belly of digastric (inserting into the digastric fossa of the mandible); the intermediate tendon is anchored to the body and greater horn of the hyoid by a fibrous pulley
intermediate tendon.a: Connects the anterior and posterior bellies of digastric and is tied to the hyoid by a fibrous loop, allowing digastric to elevate the hyoid or depress the mandible
intermediate tendon.c: The intermediate tendon pierces the insertion of stylohyoid; it is a landmark of the submandibular triangle of the neck, used at surgery to identify the hypoglossal nerve and lingual artery.

internal intercostal muscle.kid: It sits between your ribs and helps pull them down when you cough or blow out hard.
internal intercostal muscle.o: Lower border of the rib and costal cartilage above (floor of the costal groove)
internal intercostal muscle.i: Upper border of the rib and costal cartilage below
internal intercostal muscle.a: Interosseous part depresses the ribs in forced expiration; interchondral part assists elevation of the ribs in inspiration; maintains tension of the intercostal spaces
internal intercostal muscle.b: Posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal arteries (branches of the internal thoracic and musculophrenic arteries)
internal intercostal muscle.c: Its fibres run at right angles to those of the external intercostals (downward and backward); intercostal muscle strains are often caused by violent coughing or trunk twisting, with pain on deep breathing and turning.

internal oblique.kid: It is the middle layer of muscle at the side of your tummy that helps you twist and bend sideways and pulls your tummy in to protect your insides.
internal oblique.o: Thoracolumbar fascia, anterior 2/3 of the iliac crest, lateral part of the inguinal ligament
internal oblique.i: Lower borders of ribs 10–12, rectus sheath and linea alba; lower fibres insert via the conjoint tendon on the pubic crest and pecten pubis
internal oblique.a: Bilateral contraction flexes the trunk and compresses the abdominal cavity to raise intra-abdominal pressure; unilateral contraction side-bends and rotates the trunk to the same side
internal oblique.n: Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11), subcostal nerve (T12), iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1)
internal oblique.b: Superior and inferior epigastric arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery, posterior intercostal and subcostal arteries
internal oblique.c: Works together with the opposite external oblique during trunk rotation; with transversus abdominis it provides lumbar stability through the thoracolumbar fascia and is a focus of core stability training.

lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis.kid: It is in the sole of your foot near your big toe and helps the big toe bend down and push off the ground when you walk.
lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis.o: Plantar surface of the cuboid, lateral cuneiform and the extension of the tibialis posterior tendon
lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis.i: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe (the tendon contains the lateral sesamoid and attaches together with adductor hallucis)
lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis.a: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe; helps support the medial longitudinal arch
lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis.b: Medial plantar artery, first plantar metatarsal artery
lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis.c: The sesamoids within the tendons bear the load of push-off; runners and dancers can develop sesamoiditis or stress fractures, with tenderness beneath the first metatarsal head.

lateral head of gastrocnemius.kid: It is the bulgy muscle on the outer side of your calf that helps you stand on tiptoe, run and jump up high.
lateral head of gastrocnemius.o: Posterosuperior part of the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle
lateral head of gastrocnemius.i: Posterior surface of the calcaneal tuberosity via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
lateral head of gastrocnemius.b: Sural arteries (branches of the popliteal artery)
lateral head of gastrocnemius.c: Crosses both the knee and the ankle, so it must be stretched with the knee extended and the ankle dorsiflexed; a fabella is occasionally present in the tendon of the lateral head. Training is mainly straight-knee heel raises.

lateral head of triceps brachii.kid: It is on the outer back of your upper arm and helps you straighten your bent elbow hard, like pushing a door.
lateral head of triceps brachii.o: Posterior surface of the humerus, superolateral to the radial groove
lateral head of triceps brachii.c: The strongest elbow-extending head of the three, forming the horseshoe contour of the posterolateral upper arm; the radial nerve runs in the radial groove deep to the lateral head and is easily injured in humeral shaft fractures.

latissimus dorsi.kid: It is the big, wide muscle on your back that pulls your arms down and back, like swimming strokes and pull-ups.
latissimus dorsi.o: Spinous processes of T7–T12, thoracolumbar fascia (lumbar and sacral spinous processes), posterior iliac crest, lower 3–4 ribs, occasionally the inferior angle of the scapula
latissimus dorsi.i: Floor of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
latissimus dorsi.a: Shoulder extension, adduction and internal rotation; with the arms fixed, pulls the trunk upward (pull-ups, crutch walking)
latissimus dorsi.c: The main muscle for pull-ups, rowing and swimming; tightness limits shoulder flexion and increases lumbar lordosis. Important for people with spinal cord injury who use crutches or perform wheelchair transfers.

levator anguli oris.kid: It is inside your cheek and lifts the corners of your mouth when you smile.
levator anguli oris.o: Canine fossa of the maxilla (below the infraorbital foramen)
levator anguli oris.i: Angle of the mouth (modiolus), interlacing with fibres of orbicularis oris and other muscles
levator anguli oris.a: Elevates the angle of the mouth (smiling) and deepens the nasolabial fold
levator anguli oris.n: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
levator anguli oris.b: Superior labial branch of the facial artery, infraorbital artery
levator anguli oris.c: In facial nerve palsy the corner of the mouth droops on the affected side; re-education of the muscles of facial expression often uses mirror feedback to practise smiling.

levator labii superioris.kid: It is in your cheek beside your nose and lifts your upper lip to show your top teeth.
levator labii superioris.o: Infraorbital margin of the maxilla and zygomatic bone (above the infraorbital foramen)
levator labii superioris.i: Skin of the upper lip and orbicularis oris
levator labii superioris.a: Elevates and everts the upper lip and deepens the nasolabial fold
levator labii superioris.n: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
levator labii superioris.c: The infraorbital neurovascular bundle emerges from the infraorbital foramen deep to it; in facial nerve palsy rehabilitation, patients can practise showing the upper teeth.

levator labii superioris alaeque nasi.kid: It runs beside your nose and flares your nostrils and lifts your upper lip when you scrunch your nose at a bad smell.
levator labii superioris alaeque nasi.i: Major alar cartilage and skin of the ala of the nose; skin of the lateral upper lip and orbicularis oris
levator labii superioris alaeque nasi.a: Elevates the upper lip and dilates the nostril (nose wrinkling, expression of disdain)
levator labii superioris alaeque nasi.n: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
levator labii superioris alaeque nasi.c: One of the longest muscle names in the human body, nicknamed the Elvis muscle; its activity can be seen as nasal flaring during forceful inspiration.

levator scapulae.kid: It runs from your neck to your shoulder blade and pulls your shoulder up when you shrug to say "I don't know".
levator scapulae.o: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1–C4
levator scapulae.i: Upper part of the medial border of the scapula (superior angle to the root of the scapular spine)
levator scapulae.a: Elevates the scapula and rotates the glenoid downward; with the scapula fixed, side-bends and rotates the neck to the same side, and bilateral contraction assists neck extension
levator scapulae.n: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and cervical nerves (C3–C4)
levator scapulae.b: Dorsal scapular artery, transverse cervical artery, ascending cervical artery
levator scapulae.c: A common culprit in acute stiff neck and neck-shoulder ache, often with trigger points at the superior angle of the scapula; stretch by side-bending the head to the opposite side, rotating it to the opposite side and looking down toward the armpit.

linea alba.kid: It is a white band down the very middle of your tummy, from your chest to the bottom of your belly, that joins the left and right tummy muscles together.
linea alba.a: Formed by the interweaving in the midline of the aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis of both sides; separates the left and right rectus abdominis and serves as a common attachment for the abdominal muscles
linea alba.c: Widening of the linea alba from pregnancy or excessive abdominal pressure is diastasis recti, and the gap can be measured in finger widths; the linea alba has few blood vessels and is the site of midline abdominal incisions.

long head of biceps brachii.kid: It is one half of the bump that pops up on the front of your upper arm, and it helps you bend your elbow and turn your palm up.
long head of biceps brachii.o: Supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and the superior labrum
long head of biceps brachii.i: Radial tuberosity, and via the bicipital aponeurosis to the fascia of the forearm
long head of biceps brachii.a: Forearm supination and elbow flexion; assists shoulder flexion and stabilises the humeral head
long head of biceps brachii.c: The tendon runs through the intertubercular sulcus and the shoulder joint capsule and is prone to tendinitis (Speed's test, Yergason's test); when it ruptures the muscle belly drops distally to produce the Popeye sign, and it is associated with SLAP lesions.

long head of biceps femoris.kid: It is on the outer back of your thigh and helps you bend your knee and kick your leg back, which matters a lot when you sprint.
long head of biceps femoris.i: Lateral side of the head of the fibula, with some fibres to the lateral condyle of the tibia
long head of biceps femoris.a: Knee flexion and hip extension; externally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed
long head of biceps femoris.n: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
long head of biceps femoris.b: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery (profunda femoris)
long head of biceps femoris.c: The most common site of hamstring strain, usually occurring in the terminal swing phase of high-speed sprinting; Nordic hamstring eccentric training can reduce the risk of strain.

long head of triceps brachii.kid: It is on the back of your upper arm, running from your shoulder blade to your elbow, and helps straighten your elbow and pull your arm backward.
long head of triceps brachii.a: Elbow extension; assists shoulder extension and adduction, and stabilises the humeral head from below when the arm is abducted
long head of triceps brachii.c: The only one of the three heads that crosses the shoulder joint, so stretching requires full shoulder flexion with elbow flexion (hand reaching down the back); it separates the quadrangular space from the triangular space.

longissimus capitis.kid: It runs from your upper back to the bone behind your ear and helps you tip your head back or turn it to the side.
longissimus capitis.o: Transverse processes of T1–T4 or T5; articular processes of C4–C7
longissimus capitis.i: Posterior border of the mastoid process of the temporal bone
longissimus capitis.a: Bilateral contraction extends the head; unilateral contraction side-bends and rotates the head to the same side
longissimus capitis.n: Posterior rami of the cervical and upper thoracic nerves
longissimus capitis.c: Lies deep to splenius capitis and sternocleidomastoid; forward head posture keeps it continuously contracted, which may be related to cervicogenic headache.

longissimus cervicis.kid: It runs from your upper back to the bones of your neck and helps you tip your neck back or bend it to the side.
