longissimus cervicis.i: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C2–C6
longissimus cervicis.a: Bilateral contraction extends the cervical spine; unilateral contraction side-bends the neck to the same side
longissimus cervicis.n: Posterior rami of the lower cervical and upper thoracic spinal nerves
longissimus cervicis.b: Deep cervical artery, dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
longissimus cervicis.c: The cervical part of the intermediate column of erector spinae; it works with the deep neck extensors to maintain cervical posture, and poor neck extensor endurance is associated with chronic neck pain.

longissimus thoracis.kid: It is one of the longest muscles in your back, running up both sides of your spine, and it helps you stand tall with a straight back.
longissimus thoracis.o: Common tendon of erector spinae: dorsal surface of the sacrum, posterior iliac crest, lumbar spinous processes, and the lumbar transverse processes
longissimus thoracis.i: Transverse processes of all thoracic vertebrae, ribs 3–12 (between the tubercles and angles); lumbar fibres insert on the accessory and transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae
longissimus thoracis.a: Bilateral contraction extends the spine; unilateral contraction side-bends the trunk to the same side
longissimus thoracis.n: Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
longissimus thoracis.b: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries
longissimus thoracis.c: The bulkiest part of erector spinae, forming a visible ridge on either side of the spine; it is heavily loaded when lifting, and bird-dog and prone back extension exercises train its endurance.

longus capitis.kid: It hides on the front of your neck bones and helps you nod gently and tuck your chin in.
longus capitis.o: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3–C6
longus capitis.i: Inferior surface of the basilar part of the occipital bone
longus capitis.a: Flexes the head and upper cervical spine (nodding); unilateral contraction assists rotation of the head to the same side
longus capitis.n: Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C1–C3)
longus capitis.b: Ascending cervical artery, ascending pharyngeal artery
longus capitis.c: One of the deep neck flexors; often weak after whiplash injury, with sternocleidomastoid compensating. The chin-tuck nodding exercise (craniocervical flexion) is the main form of training.

lower head of lateral pterygoid.kid: It is deep in your cheek and helps you open your mouth and move your jaw forward and from side to side.
lower head of lateral pterygoid.o: Lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate of the sphenoid
lower head of lateral pterygoid.i: Pterygoid fovea on the neck of the condylar process of the mandible
lower head of lateral pterygoid.a: Bilateral contraction protrudes the mandible and opens the mouth (pulls the condyle forward); unilateral contraction moves the mandible to the opposite side
lower head of lateral pterygoid.n: Nerve to lateral pterygoid from the mandibular nerve (CN V3)
lower head of lateral pterygoid.b: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery
lower head of lateral pterygoid.c: The only muscle of mastication mainly responsible for opening the mouth; excessive tension or spasm is associated with temporomandibular disorders and deviation on opening, and it can be palpated intraorally behind the upper molars.

lumbar rotator.kid: It is a tiny muscle on the bones of your lower back that works like a little sensor telling your brain where your back is.
lumbar rotator.o: Mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae (at the root of the transverse processes)
lumbar rotator.i: Lamina and root of the spinous process of the vertebra one or two levels above
lumbar rotator.a: Segmental stabilisation of the spine and proprioception; assists spinal extension and rotation to the opposite side
lumbar rotator.n: Medial branches of the posterior rami of the spinal nerves
lumbar rotator.b: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries
lumbar rotator.c: The deepest layer of the transversospinalis group, often poorly developed or absent in the lumbar region; rich in muscle spindles, its role is more position-sense feedback than torque production.

medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.kid: It is in the sole of your foot at the base of your big toe and helps the big toe bend down and hold you up when you stand on tiptoe.
medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.o: Plantar surface of the cuboid, lateral cuneiform and the extension of the tibialis posterior tendon
medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.i: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe (the tendon contains the medial sesamoid and attaches together with abductor hallucis)
medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.a: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe; helps support the medial longitudinal arch
medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.b: Medial plantar artery, first plantar metatarsal artery
medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.c: The medial (tibial) sesamoid bears more load and is more often affected by sesamoiditis; a plantar plate injury from hyperdorsiflexion of the great toe is called turf toe.

medial head of gastrocnemius.kid: It is the big muscle on the inner side of your calf that helps you stand on tiptoe, run and jump up hard.
medial head of gastrocnemius.o: Posterosuperior part of the medial femoral condyle and the popliteal surface above it
medial head of gastrocnemius.i: Posterior surface of the calcaneal tuberosity via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
medial head of gastrocnemius.b: Sural arteries (branches of the popliteal artery)
medial head of gastrocnemius.c: A strain at the musculotendinous junction of the medial head is called tennis leg, often occurring with a sudden push-off; it must be distinguished from deep vein thrombosis and Achilles tendon rupture.

medial head of triceps brachii.kid: It hides deep in the back of your upper arm and pitches in every time you straighten your elbow, whether the job is light or heavy.
medial head of triceps brachii.o: Posterior surface of the humerus inferomedial to the radial groove; medial and lateral intermuscular septa
medial head of triceps brachii.a: Elbow extension (active at all speeds and loads; the workhorse of elbow extension)
medial head of triceps brachii.b: Deep brachial artery (profunda brachii), superior ulnar collateral artery
medial head of triceps brachii.c: Lies deep to the long and lateral heads and is also called the deep head; it is recruited first even in lightly loaded elbow extension, and some fibres insert into the elbow joint capsule to prevent the capsule being pinched.

medial pterygoid.kid: It is on the inner side of your jawbone and helps you close your mouth tight and grind up food when you bite.
medial pterygoid.o: Deep head: medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate of the sphenoid and pyramidal process of the palatine bone; superficial head: tuberosity of the maxilla
medial pterygoid.i: Pterygoid tuberosity on the medial surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible
medial pterygoid.a: Elevates the mandible (closes the mouth) and assists protrusion; unilateral contraction moves the mandible to the opposite side (grinding)
medial pterygoid.n: Nerve to medial pterygoid from the mandibular nerve (CN V3)
medial pterygoid.b: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery
medial pterygoid.c: Forms a sling with masseter on the inner and outer sides of the angle of the mandible; spasm can cause trismus, it can be palpated medial to the angle of the mandible or intraorally, and it is commonly involved in temporomandibular disorders.

mentalis.kid: It is on your chin and pushes your lower lip up and wrinkles your chin when you pout or are about to cry.
mentalis.a: Elevates and protrudes the lower lip and wrinkles the skin of the chin (pouting, expression of doubt)
mentalis.n: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
mentalis.c: People who have difficulty closing their lips (e.g. mouth breathers or those with protruding teeth) often overuse mentalis, giving the chin a golf-ball dimpled appearance, a key observation in orofacial myofunctional assessment.

multifidus.kid: It is a row of little muscle pieces hugging your spine that hold each backbone steady, like tiny screws.
multifidus.o: Dorsal surface of the sacrum, posterior superior iliac spine, mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae, transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae, articular processes of C4–C7
multifidus.i: Spinous processes of the vertebrae 2–4 levels above
multifidus.a: Segmental stabilisation of the spine; bilateral contraction extends the spine, unilateral contraction rotates the spine to the opposite side and assists side-bending to the same side
multifidus.n: Medial branches of the posterior rami of the spinal nerves
multifidus.b: Dorsal branches of the lumbar, posterior intercostal and deep cervical arteries
multifidus.c: Segmental atrophy and fatty infiltration are common after low back pain and do not recover spontaneously; it can be palpated beside the lumbar spinous processes and trained with stabilisation exercises using co-contraction with transversus abdominis.

mylohyoid.kid: It spreads like a hammock across the bottom of your mouth and lifts your tongue and the floor of your mouth when you swallow.
mylohyoid.o: Mylohyoid line on the inner surface of the mandible
mylohyoid.i: Median fibrous raphe and body of the hyoid bone
mylohyoid.a: Elevates the hyoid, floor of the mouth and tongue (swallowing and speech); with the hyoid fixed, assists depression of the mandible
mylohyoid.n: Nerve to mylohyoid (branch of the inferior alveolar nerve, CN V3)
mylohyoid.b: Mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery, submental artery
mylohyoid.c: Forms the muscular diaphragm of the floor of the mouth; its contraction can be felt under the chin during swallowing, and surface electromyography at this site is often used as feedback in dysphagia assessment.

nasalis.kid: It covers your nose and can make your nostrils smaller or wider, so your nose moves when you breathe in hard.
nasalis.o: Maxilla (superolateral to the canine eminence and beside the nasal notch)
nasalis.i: Transverse part: aponeurosis over the dorsum of the nose; alar part: major alar cartilage and skin of the ala of the nose
nasalis.a: Transverse part compresses the nostril; alar part dilates the nostril (nasal flaring)
nasalis.n: Buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
nasalis.b: Lateral nasal branch of the facial artery, infraorbital artery
nasalis.c: Nasal flaring seen in respiratory distress is a clinical sign used to assess the work of breathing, and is especially obvious in infants and young children.

oblique head of adductor hallucis.kid: It lies slantwise deep in the sole of your foot, pulls your big toe toward the other toes and helps hold up the arch of your foot.
oblique head of adductor hallucis.o: Bases of metatarsals 2–4; sheath of the fibularis (peroneus) longus tendon
oblique head of adductor hallucis.i: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe (via the lateral sesamoid, attaching together with the lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis)
oblique head of adductor hallucis.a: Adducts the great toe (pulls it toward the 2nd toe) and assists flexion of the metatarsophalangeal joint; maintains the transverse arch of the foot
oblique head of adductor hallucis.n: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
oblique head of adductor hallucis.b: Plantar arterial arch, first plantar metatarsal artery
oblique head of adductor hallucis.c: In hallux valgus the pull of this muscle worsens the lateral deviation of the great toe, and surgical correction often requires release of its tendon; conservative treatment strengthens abductor hallucis to balance it.

oblique head of adductor pollicis.kid: It squeezes your thumb in toward your palm so you can pinch a piece of paper or a key really hard.
oblique head of adductor pollicis.o: Capitate; bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals
oblique head of adductor pollicis.i: Ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb (via the ulnar sesamoid) and the extensor expansion
oblique head of adductor pollicis.a: Thumb adduction; assists flexion of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint and lateral (key) pinch
oblique head of adductor pollicis.n: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
oblique head of adductor pollicis.c: With ulnar nerve injury the adductor pollicis is weak, so pinching a sheet of paper is compensated by flexor pollicis longus, producing Froment's sign.

obliquus capitis inferior.kid: A little muscle hidden under the back of your head that helps you turn your head left or right.
obliquus capitis inferior.a: Rotates the head to the same side at the atlantoaxial joint
obliquus capitis inferior.b: Vertebral artery; descending branch of the occipital artery
obliquus capitis inferior.c: One of the suboccipital muscles, forming the inferior border of the suboccipital triangle; the greater occipital nerve curves around its lower border, and tightness may be related to cervicogenic headache.

obliquus capitis superior.kid: A little muscle under the back of your head that helps you tip your head back a bit and tilt it to the side.
obliquus capitis superior.i: Lateral part of the occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines
obliquus capitis superior.a: Head extension and ipsilateral lateral flexion at the atlanto-occipital joint
obliquus capitis superior.b: Vertebral artery; descending branch of the occipital artery
obliquus capitis superior.c: The suboccipital muscles are rich in muscle spindles and are mainly responsible for fine control of head posture; they readily become shortened and tight in a forward head posture.

obturator externus.kid: A muscle hiding deep in your bottom that helps you turn your thigh and toes outward.
obturator externus.o: External surface of the obturator membrane and the pubic and ischial bony margins around the obturator foramen
obturator externus.a: Hip external rotation; assists adduction and stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
obturator externus.n: Posterior branch of the obturator nerve (L3–L4)
obturator externus.b: Obturator artery; medial circumflex femoral artery
obturator externus.c: Its tendon passes below and behind the femoral neck; it is one of the deep external rotators of the hip and lies too deep to palpate directly with ease.

obturator internus.kid: A muscle that wraps out from inside your pelvis and helps you turn your thigh outward and stand more steadily.
obturator internus.o: Pelvic surface of the obturator membrane and the bony margins around the obturator foramen
obturator internus.i: Medial surface of the greater trochanter of the femur (exits through the lesser sciatic foramen and inserts here together with the superior and inferior gemelli)
obturator internus.a: External rotation with the hip extended, abduction with the hip flexed; stabilises the femoral head
obturator internus.b: Internal pudendal artery; inferior gluteal artery; obturator artery
obturator internus.c: Its fascia gives attachment to the tendinous arch of levator ani, so it is closely tied to pelvic floor function; it can be palpated by internal vaginal or rectal examination.

occipitalis.kid: A thin muscle at the back of your head that pulls your scalp backward and helps you raise your eyebrows.
occipitalis.o: Lateral two-thirds of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone; mastoid process of the temporal bone
occipitalis.a: Pulls the scalp backward and anchors the epicranial aponeurosis to help frontalis raise the eyebrows
occipitalis.n: Posterior auricular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
occipitalis.c: A common tender point in tension-type headache; it can be palpated and released along the lateral part of the superior nuchal line.

omohyoid.kid: A long, thin muscle running from your shoulder to your throat that helps pull your throat back down after you swallow.
omohyoid.o: Superior border of the scapula (medial to the scapular notch; origin of the inferior belly)
omohyoid.i: Lower border of the body of the hyoid bone (insertion of the superior belly); the intermediate tendon is anchored to the clavicle by a fascial sling
omohyoid.a: Depresses, retracts and fixes the hyoid bone; stabilises the hyoid during swallowing and phonation
omohyoid.b: Superior thyroid artery; branches of the lingual artery
omohyoid.c: One of the infrahyoid muscles, with superior and inferior bellies and an intermediate tendon; the inferior belly crosses the posterior triangle of the neck obliquely and is an important landmark in the neck.

opponens digiti minimi of foot.kid: A little muscle on the outer side of the sole of your foot that helps the little-toe side of your foot bend down a bit.
opponens digiti minimi of foot.o: Base of the 5th metatarsal; sheath of the fibularis longus tendon (often regarded as the deep fibres of flexor digiti minimi brevis)
opponens digiti minimi of foot.a: Pulls the 5th metatarsal plantarward and medially; helps maintain the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot
opponens digiti minimi of foot.n: Superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
opponens digiti minimi of foot.c: This muscle is often fused with flexor digiti minimi brevis or absent, with wide individual variation.

opponens digiti minimi of hand.kid: It brings your little finger in toward your palm so it can touch your thumb and your hand can make a bowl shape.
opponens digiti minimi of hand.o: Hook of the hamate; flexor retinaculum
opponens digiti minimi of hand.i: Whole length of the ulnar border of the 5th metacarpal
opponens digiti minimi of hand.a: Opposition of the little finger: draws the 5th metacarpal forward and rotates it, deepening the hollow of the palm
opponens digiti minimi of hand.n: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
opponens digiti minimi of hand.b: Deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
opponens digiti minimi of hand.c: The deepest of the hypothenar muscles; with ulnar nerve injury the hypothenar eminence wastes and grip strength and the palmar arch are reduced.

opponens pollicis.kid: It lets your thumb turn around to touch your other fingers, so you can pinch things and hold a pencil.
opponens pollicis.o: Tubercle of the trapezium; flexor retinaculum
opponens pollicis.i: Whole length of the radial border of the 1st metacarpal
opponens pollicis.a: Opposition of the thumb: flexes and medially rotates the 1st metacarpal
opponens pollicis.n: Recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8–T1)
opponens pollicis.b: Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
opponens pollicis.c: In severe carpal tunnel syndrome the thenar eminence wastes and opposition is weak; test resisted pad-to-pad pinch between the thumb and little finger.

orbicularis oris.kid: The ring of muscle around your mouth that lets you close your lips, pout, whistle and give kisses.
orbicularis oris.o: Median parts of the maxilla and mandible, the modiolus and the deep perioral skin
orbicularis oris.i: Skin and mucous membrane of the lips
orbicularis oris.a: Closes and purses (protrudes) the lips and presses them against the teeth; assists chewing and articulation
orbicularis oris.n: Buccal and marginal mandibular branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
orbicularis oris.b: Superior and inferior labial arteries of the facial artery
orbicularis oris.c: In facial nerve palsy the patient cannot seal the lips or puff out the cheeks, air leaks when blowing and saliva drools; it is a key focus of facial muscle re-education.

orbital part of orbicularis oculi.kid: The muscle around the outside of your eye that lets you squeeze your eyes shut really tight.
orbital part of orbicularis oculi.o: Nasal part of the frontal bone; frontal process of the maxilla; medial canthal (palpebral) ligament
orbital part of orbicularis oculi.i: Encircles the orbit and returns to the region of the medial canthus; also attaches to the skin around the orbit
orbital part of orbicularis oculi.a: Forcefully closes the eyelids tightly, protecting the eyeball
orbital part of orbicularis oculi.n: Temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
orbital part of orbicularis oculi.b: Facial artery, superficial temporal artery and branches of the ophthalmic artery
orbital part of orbicularis oculi.c: In facial nerve palsy the eye cannot close fully (lagophthalmos), so corneal protection is needed; its contraction forms crow's feet.

palmaris longus.kid: A long, skinny muscle in your forearm that helps bend your wrist toward your palm and pulls the skin of your palm tight.
palmaris longus.o: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
palmaris longus.i: Distal part of the flexor retinaculum and the palmar aponeurosis
palmaris longus.a: Wrist flexion (weak); tenses the palmar aponeurosis
palmaris longus.c: Absent on one or both sides in about 15% of people; the tendon stands out when the thumb and little finger are opposed with the wrist flexed, it is often used as a tendon graft, and the median nerve lies deep and lateral to it.

palpebral part of orbicularis oculi.kid: A thin muscle inside your eyelids that lets you blink gently and keep your eyes closed when you sleep.
palpebral part of orbicularis oculi.a: Gently closes the eyelids (blinking, eye closure during sleep)
palpebral part of orbicularis oculi.n: Temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
palpebral part of orbicularis oculi.b: Facial artery, superficial temporal artery and branches of the ophthalmic artery
palpebral part of orbicularis oculi.c: Blinking spreads tears evenly over the cornea; in facial nerve palsy the blink reflex is reduced and the eye dries out easily.

pectineus.kid: A muscle on the inside of the top of your thigh that helps you squeeze your legs together and also helps lift your thigh.
pectineus.o: Pecten pubis on the superior pubic ramus
pectineus.i: Pectineal line of the femur (below the lesser trochanter)
pectineus.n: Femoral nerve (L2–L3); sometimes also supplied by the obturator nerve
pectineus.b: Medial circumflex femoral artery; obturator artery
pectineus.c: Forms the medial part of the floor of the femoral triangle; one of the common sites of groin strain, palpable just medial to the femoral pulse.

pectoralis minor.kid: A muscle hidden under the big chest muscle that pulls your shoulder forward and down and also helps you breathe in.
pectoralis minor.o: Anterior surfaces of ribs 3–5 (near the costal cartilages)
pectoralis minor.i: Medial border and superior surface of the coracoid process of the scapula
pectoralis minor.a: Scapular protraction, depression, downward rotation and anterior tilt; with the scapula fixed, elevates the ribs to assist inspiration
pectoralis minor.b: Pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery; lateral thoracic artery
pectoralis minor.c: Shortening causes rounded shoulders and anterior scapular tilt and may compress the brachial plexus and axillary artery beneath it (pectoralis minor syndrome); it is commonly stretched in supine or in a doorway.

piriformis.kid: A pear-shaped muscle deep in your bottom that helps you turn your thigh outward and stay steady when you walk.
piriformis.o: Anterior surface of the sacrum (lateral to the 2nd–4th anterior sacral foramina)
piriformis.i: Superior border of the greater trochanter of the femur
piriformis.a: External rotation with the hip extended; abduction with the hip flexed (becomes an internal rotator beyond about 90° of hip flexion); stabilises the femoral head
piriformis.b: Superior gluteal artery; inferior gluteal artery
piriformis.c: The sciatic nerve usually emerges at its lower border, and a tight or hypertrophied muscle can cause piriformis syndrome; it is commonly stretched in the figure-4 position (hip flexion, adduction and external rotation).

plantaris.kid: A long, skinny little muscle at the back of your lower leg that helps a tiny bit with standing on tiptoe and bending your knee.
plantaris.o: Lower end of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur; oblique popliteal ligament
plantaris.i: Calcaneal tuberosity (its long slender tendon runs along the medial side of the Achilles tendon to the calcaneus)
plantaris.a: Weakly assists ankle plantarflexion and knee flexion
plantaris.b: Sural arteries of the popliteal artery
plantaris.c: Absent in about 7–10% of people; tendon rupture (tennis leg) presents much like a strain of the medial head of gastrocnemius, and the tendon is also often used as graft material.

platysma.kid: A very thin sheet of muscle at the front of your neck that pulls the corners of your mouth down and tightens your neck when you make a funny face.
platysma.o: Fascia covering the upper parts of pectoralis major and deltoid
platysma.i: Lower border of the mandible, skin of the lower face and the angle of the mouth
platysma.a: Draws the lower lip and angle of the mouth downward and tenses the skin of the neck; assists depression of the mandible
platysma.n: Cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
platysma.c: A cutaneous muscle; with facial nerve injury the skin of the neck on the affected side cannot be tensed, which can be used as an examination item.

popliteus.kid: A little muscle behind your knee that works like a key, unlocking your straight, locked knee so it can bend again.
popliteus.o: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle; posterior horn of the lateral meniscus
popliteus.i: Posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line
popliteus.a: Unlocks the extended knee (internally rotates the tibia in open chain, externally rotates the femur in closed chain); weak knee flexion; pulls the lateral meniscus posteriorly during knee flexion
popliteus.b: Medial and lateral inferior genicular arteries of the popliteal artery
popliteus.c: An important dynamic stabiliser of the posterolateral corner of the knee; downhill running readily provokes popliteus tendinopathy, presenting as posterolateral knee pain.

posterior belly of digastric.kid: A muscle running from behind your ear to your throat that helps when you swallow and when you open your mouth.
posterior belly of digastric.o: Mastoid notch of the temporal bone
posterior belly of digastric.i: Intermediate tendon (attached to the body and greater horn of the hyoid by a fibrous pulley)
posterior belly of digastric.a: Elevates and retracts the hyoid bone; with the hyoid fixed, assists depression of the mandible (mouth opening)
posterior belly of digastric.n: Digastric branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
posterior belly of digastric.c: Its nerve supply differs from that of the anterior belly (mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve); it is an important landmark in neck surgery for identifying the internal jugular vein and the cranial nerves.

procerus.kid: A little muscle between your two eyebrows that you use when you wrinkle your nose or frown because you are cross.
procerus.o: Fascia over the lower part of the nasal bone and the upper part of the lateral nasal cartilage
procerus.a: Draws the medial end of the eyebrow downward, producing transverse wrinkles over the root of the nose
procerus.n: Temporal and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
procerus.b: Angular artery of the facial artery

pronator quadratus.kid: A square muscle deep down just above your wrist that helps you turn your palm over to face down.
pronator quadratus.o: Anterior surface of the distal quarter of the ulna
pronator quadratus.i: Anterior surface of the distal quarter of the radius
pronator quadratus.a: Forearm pronation (the principal pronator); deep fibres stabilise the distal radioulnar joint
pronator quadratus.n: Anterior interosseous nerve of the median nerve (C8–T1)
pronator quadratus.c: With the elbow flexed beyond 90° pronator teres is shortened, allowing pronator quadratus to be tested in relative isolation; it is weak in anterior interosseous nerve syndrome.

psoas major.kid: A big muscle running from the bones of your lower back to your thigh that helps you lift your leg to walk and climb stairs.
psoas major.o: Sides of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs of T12–L5; transverse processes of L1–L5
psoas major.i: Lesser trochanter of the femur (joins iliacus to form iliopsoas)
psoas major.a: Hip flexion (the strongest hip flexor); flexes the trunk when the lower limb is fixed; unilateral contraction laterally flexes the lumbar spine to the same side
psoas major.n: Anterior rami of the lumbar plexus (L1–L3)
psoas major.b: Lumbar arteries; lumbar branch of the iliolumbar artery
psoas major.c: Prone to shortening with prolonged sitting, causing increased lumbar lordosis and low back pain; tightness is assessed with the Thomas test, and it is commonly stretched in a lunge position.

pubococcygeus.kid: A hammock-like muscle at the bottom of your pelvis that holds up the organs in your tummy and also helps you hold in your pee.
pubococcygeus.o: Posterior surface of the body of the pubis; anterior part of the tendinous arch of levator ani
pubococcygeus.i: Anococcygeal ligament, coccyx and perineal body
pubococcygeus.a: Supports the pelvic viscera and resists rises in intra-abdominal pressure; assists control of urination and defecation
pubococcygeus.n: Nerve to levator ani (S3–S4); branches of the pudendal nerve
pubococcygeus.b: Inferior gluteal artery; internal pudendal artery
pubococcygeus.c: The main part of levator ani and the principal target of Kegel exercises; after childbirth or when weak, stress urinary incontinence and organ prolapse readily occur.

puborectalis.kid: A muscle that hooks around your rectum like a sling, helping you hold in your poo and only relaxing when you go to the toilet.
puborectalis.o: Posterior surface of the body of the pubis
puborectalis.i: Passes behind the anorectal junction and joins the fibres of the opposite side to form a U-shaped sling
puborectalis.a: Pulls the anorectal junction forward to maintain the anorectal angle and control defecation; relaxes during defecation
puborectalis.n: Nerve to levator ani (S3–S4); inferior rectal nerve of the pudendal nerve
puborectalis.b: Internal pudendal artery; inferior gluteal artery
puborectalis.c: Failure to relax, or even paradoxical contraction, during defecation (pelvic floor dyssynergia) causes outlet-obstruction constipation, which can be treated with biofeedback training.

pyramidalis.kid: A little triangle-shaped muscle at the very bottom of your tummy that helps pull the line down the middle of your tummy tight.
pyramidalis.o: Pubic crest and the front of the pubic symphysis
pyramidalis.i: Linea alba (between the umbilicus and the pubis)
pyramidalis.c: Lies within the rectus sheath, in front of the lower end of rectus abdominis; absent in about 20% of people.

quadratus femoris.kid: A square muscle deep in your bottom that helps you turn your thigh outward and keeps your hip joint steadier.
quadratus femoris.o: Lateral border of the ischial tuberosity
quadratus femoris.i: Quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest of the femur
quadratus femoris.a: Hip external rotation; assists adduction and stabilises the femoral head
quadratus femoris.b: Medial circumflex femoral artery; inferior gluteal artery
quadratus femoris.c: When the space between the ischium and the lesser trochanter is too narrow it can be impinged (ischiofemoral impingement syndrome), causing deep gluteal pain.

quadratus lumborum.kid: A square muscle on each side of your lower back that helps you bend your body sideways and keeps your lower back steady.
quadratus lumborum.o: Medial part of the posterior iliac crest; iliolumbar ligament
quadratus lumborum.i: Medial half of the lower border of the 12th rib; transverse processes of L1–L4
quadratus lumborum.a: Unilateral: lateral flexion of the trunk to the same side, elevation of the pelvis on the same side; bilateral: extends and stabilises the lumbar spine and fixes the 12th rib during inspiration
quadratus lumborum.n: Anterior rami of T12 and L1–L4
quadratus lumborum.b: Lumbar arteries; lumbar branch of the iliolumbar artery; subcostal artery
quadratus lumborum.c: A common source of tender points in low back pain; the side plank is a frequently used exercise, and it can be stretched by side bending in side-lying or standing.

radial head of flexor digitorum superfic.kid: A muscle in your forearm that helps bend your fingers so you can make a fist and grab things.
radial head of flexor digitorum superfic.o: Upper half of the anterior border of the radius (oblique line of the radius)
radial head of flexor digitorum superfic.i: Both sides of the shafts of the middle phalanges of digits 2–5
radial head of flexor digitorum superfic.a: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints; continues to flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and assists wrist flexion
radial head of flexor digitorum superfic.c: The median nerve and ulnar artery pass beneath the tendinous arch between the humeroulnar and radial heads, a potential site of nerve entrapment; to test it in isolation, hold the other fingers in extension.

rectus abdominis.kid: The muscle at the front of your tummy that looks like a row of blocks and helps you do sit-ups and bend your body forward.
rectus abdominis.i: Costal cartilages of ribs 5–7; xiphoid process of the sternum
rectus abdominis.a: Trunk flexion and posterior pelvic tilt; raises intra-abdominal pressure and assists forced expiration
rectus abdominis.b: Superior epigastric artery; inferior epigastric artery
rectus abdominis.c: Divided into several segments by tendinous intersections (the six-pack); diastasis recti is common after pregnancy and can be assessed by palpating the width of the linea alba during a curl-up.

rectus capitis anterior.kid: A little muscle deep at the front of the very top of your neck that helps you gently nod 'yes'.
rectus capitis anterior.o: Anterior surface of the lateral mass of the atlas (C1) and the root of its transverse process
rectus capitis anterior.i: Basilar part of the occipital bone (in front of the foramen magnum)
rectus capitis anterior.a: Flexion at the atlanto-occipital joint (nodding); stabilises the atlanto-occipital joint
rectus capitis anterior.c: One of the deep neck flexors and one of the target muscles of craniocervical flexion (chin-tuck nodding) training.

rectus capitis lateralis.kid: A little muscle at the side of the very top of your neck that helps you tilt your head slightly to the same side.
rectus capitis lateralis.o: Superior surface of the transverse process of the atlas (C1)
rectus capitis lateralis.i: Jugular process of the occipital bone
rectus capitis lateralis.a: Ipsilateral lateral flexion of the head; stabilises the atlanto-occipital joint

rectus capitis posterior major.kid: A little muscle under the back of your head that helps you tip your head back and can also turn your head to the same side.
rectus capitis posterior major.i: Lateral part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone
rectus capitis posterior major.b: Vertebral artery; descending branch of the occipital artery
rectus capitis posterior major.c: Forms the superomedial border of the suboccipital triangle; chronically shortened in a forward head posture, it is the main target of suboccipital release techniques.

rectus capitis posterior minor.kid: The tiniest muscle right under the back of your head that helps you tip your head back a little and feel where your head is.
rectus capitis posterior minor.i: Medial part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone
rectus capitis posterior minor.a: Head extension at the atlanto-occipital joint; provides proprioception of head position
rectus capitis posterior minor.b: Vertebral artery; descending branch of the occipital artery
rectus capitis posterior minor.c: It is connected to the spinal dura mater by connective tissue (the myodural bridge), which is thought to be related to cervicogenic headache.

rectus femoris.kid: The long muscle right at the front of your thigh that helps you kick a ball, straighten your knee and lift your thigh.
rectus femoris.o: Anterior inferior iliac spine (straight head); upper margin of the acetabulum (reflected head)
rectus femoris.i: Patella via the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament
rectus femoris.a: Knee extension; hip flexion (the only part of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint)
rectus femoris.b: Descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery
rectus femoris.c: Commonly strained in kicking and sprinting, and adolescents can sustain an avulsion fracture of the anterior inferior iliac spine; tightness is assessed with the Ely test, and stretching requires hip extension combined with knee flexion.

rhomboid major.kid: A muscle between your two shoulder blades on your back that helps you squeeze your shoulders back and stand up tall.
rhomboid major.o: Spinous processes of T2–T5 and the supraspinous ligament
rhomboid major.i: Medial border of the scapula (from the root of the scapular spine to the inferior angle)
rhomboid major.a: Scapular retraction, elevation and downward rotation; holds the scapula against the thoracic wall
rhomboid major.c: Often lengthened and weak in a rounded-shoulder, kyphotic posture; trained with rowing and scapular retraction exercises, and strength can be tested by placing the back of the hand on the low back and lifting it away backward.

rhomboid minor.kid: A little helper sitting above the big rhomboid muscle that works with it to pull your shoulder blade back toward your spine.
rhomboid minor.o: Lower part of the ligamentum nuchae; spinous processes of C7–T1
rhomboid minor.i: Medial border of the scapula at the root of the scapular spine
rhomboid minor.a: Scapular retraction, elevation and downward rotation
rhomboid minor.c: Lies deep to trapezius and is often fused with rhomboid major; aching along the upper part of the medial border of the scapula is often related to this muscle and levator scapulae.

risorius.kid: A thin muscle in your cheek that pulls the corners of your mouth out to the sides so you can smile.
risorius.i: Skin at the angle of the mouth and the modiolus
risorius.a: Draws the angle of the mouth laterally (smiling, grinning)
risorius.n: Buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)

sartorius.kid: The longest muscle in your whole body, running slantwise across your thigh, that helps you sit cross-legged and cross one leg over the other.
sartorius.i: Medial surface of the proximal tibia (pes anserinus)
sartorius.a: Hip flexion, abduction and external rotation; knee flexion, and assists internal rotation of the leg when the knee is flexed
sartorius.b: Muscular branches of the femoral artery
sartorius.c: Forms the pes anserinus together with gracilis and semitendinosus, and pes anserine bursitis causes pain below the medial side of the knee; its medial border is the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle.

scalenus anterior.kid: A muscle at the side of your neck that pulls your first rib up when you take a deep breath and also helps your neck bend sideways.
scalenus anterior.o: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3–C6
scalenus anterior.a: Elevates the 1st rib (accessory inspiration); unilaterally flexes the cervical spine laterally to the same side, bilaterally flexes the cervical spine forward
scalenus anterior.n: Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C4–C6)
scalenus anterior.b: Ascending cervical artery (branch of the inferior thyroid artery)
scalenus anterior.c: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass through the interscalene space between the anterior and middle scalenes, and tightness can cause thoracic outlet syndrome; the phrenic nerve runs on its anterior surface.

scalenus medius.kid: The biggest of the scalene muscles at the side of your neck that helps you tilt your head toward your shoulder and lifts your ribs when you breathe in.
scalenus medius.o: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C2–C7
scalenus medius.i: Superior surface of the 1st rib (behind the groove for the subclavian artery)
scalenus medius.a: Elevates the 1st rib (accessory inspiration); ipsilateral lateral flexion of the cervical spine
scalenus medius.n: Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C3–C8)
scalenus medius.b: Ascending cervical artery; transverse cervical artery
scalenus medius.c: The dorsal scapular nerve and long thoracic nerve often pierce this muscle and may be entrapped here; to stretch it, laterally flex the neck to the opposite side while fixing the 1st rib.

scalenus posterior.kid: A little muscle at the back of the side of your neck that helps lift your second rib and also lets your neck bend sideways.
scalenus posterior.o: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C5–C7
scalenus posterior.a: Elevates the 2nd rib (accessory inspiration); ipsilateral lateral flexion of the cervical spine
scalenus posterior.n: Anterior rami of the cervical nerves (C6–C8)
scalenus posterior.b: Ascending cervical artery; transverse cervical artery
scalenus posterior.c: In people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or a habitual chest-breathing pattern, the scalene group is often overused and tight.

second lumbrical of foot.kid: A little worm-like muscle in the sole of your foot that helps your third toe bend where it joins the foot while its tip stays straight.
second lumbrical of foot.o: Adjacent sides of the flexor digitorum longus tendons to the 2nd and 3rd toes
second lumbrical of foot.i: Medial side of the proximal phalanx of the 3rd toe and the extensor expansion
second lumbrical of foot.a: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints of the 3rd toe
second lumbrical of foot.n: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
second lumbrical of foot.b: Lateral plantar artery; plantar metatarsal arteries
second lumbrical of foot.c: When the intrinsic foot muscles are weak, the metatarsophalangeal joints hyperextend and the interphalangeal joints flex, forming claw toes; train with short foot and towel-curl exercises.

second plantar interosseous of foot.kid: A little muscle between the bones of your foot that pulls your fourth toe in toward your second toe.
second plantar interosseous of foot.o: Base and medial surface of the 4th metatarsal
second plantar interosseous of foot.i: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the 4th toe and the extensor expansion
second plantar interosseous of foot.a: Adduction of the 4th toe (toward the 2nd toe); flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and assists extension of the interphalangeal joints
second plantar interosseous of foot.n: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
second plantar interosseous of foot.b: Lateral plantar artery; plantar metatarsal arteries
second plantar interosseous of foot.c: The interossei of the foot are arranged around the 2nd toe as the axis (in the hand the axis is the middle finger); they help stabilise the forefoot during push-off.

semimembranosus.kid: A muscle on the inner back of your thigh that helps you bend your knee and also stretch your thigh backward.
semimembranosus.o: Superolateral aspect of the ischial tuberosity
semimembranosus.i: Posterior surface of the medial condyle of the tibia (with an expansion forming the oblique popliteal ligament)
semimembranosus.a: Hip extension and knee flexion; internally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed
semimembranosus.n: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
semimembranosus.b: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery; branches of the popliteal artery
semimembranosus.c: One of the hamstrings, lying deep to semitendinosus; swelling of the bursa between it and the medial head of gastrocnemius is a Baker's cyst.

semispinalis capitis.kid: A thick muscle at the back of your neck that helps you lift your head to look up and holds up your heavy head.
semispinalis capitis.o: Articular processes of C4–C6; transverse processes of C7–T6
semispinalis capitis.i: Medial part of the occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines
semispinalis capitis.a: Bilateral: extension of the head and neck; unilateral: ipsilateral lateral flexion of the head with slight rotation to the opposite side
semispinalis capitis.n: Posterior rami of the cervical and upper thoracic nerves
semispinalis capitis.b: Descending branch of the occipital artery; deep cervical artery
semispinalis capitis.c: The bulkiest extensor at the back of the neck, forming the longitudinal bulge on each side of the posterior neck; the greater occipital nerve pierces it, and tightness can cause occipital headache.

semispinalis cervicis.kid: A muscle deep in the back of your neck that helps you straighten your neck backward and keep it steady.
semispinalis cervicis.i: Spinous processes of C2–C5 (mainly the spinous process of the axis)
semispinalis cervicis.a: Bilateral: extension of the cervical spine; unilateral: rotation of the cervical spine to the opposite side
semispinalis cervicis.n: Posterior rami of the cervical and upper thoracic nerves
semispinalis cervicis.b: Deep cervical artery; descending branch of the occipital artery; posterior intercostal arteries
semispinalis cervicis.c: A deep neck extensor; atrophy and under-activation are common in patients with neck pain, making it a target muscle for cervical stabilisation training.

semispinalis thoracis.kid: A muscle deep beside the spine in your upper back that helps you straighten your back and also helps your body twist.
semispinalis thoracis.a: Bilateral: extension of the thoracic and lower cervical spine; unilateral: rotation of the spine to the opposite side
semispinalis thoracis.n: Posterior rami of the thoracic nerves
semispinalis thoracis.b: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
semispinalis thoracis.c: The most superficial layer of the transversospinalis group; each fascicle spans about 4–6 vertebral segments.

semitendinosus.kid: A long muscle on the inner back of your thigh that helps you bend your knee and kick your leg back when you run.
semitendinosus.o: Ischial tuberosity (common tendon with the long head of biceps femoris)
semitendinosus.i: Medial surface of the proximal tibia (pes anserinus)
semitendinosus.a: Hip extension and knee flexion; internally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed
semitendinosus.n: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
semitendinosus.b: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery; inferior gluteal artery
semitendinosus.c: Its tendon is often harvested as a graft for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction; during resisted knee flexion a prominent cord-like tendon can be felt at the posteromedial knee.

serratus anterior.kid: A muscle beside your ribs that looks like the teeth of a saw and pushes your shoulder blade forward when you punch or push things.
serratus anterior.i: Anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula (superior angle to inferior angle)
serratus anterior.a: Scapular protraction and upward rotation; holds the medial border of the scapula against the thoracic wall
serratus anterior.c: Long thoracic nerve injury or muscle weakness causes scapular winging, most obvious when pushing against a wall; commonly trained with the push-up plus, wall slides and similar exercises.

serratus posterior inferior.kid: A thin, saw-toothed muscle in your lower back that pulls your lower ribs down when you breathe out hard.
serratus posterior inferior.o: Spinous processes of T11–L2 (via the thoracolumbar fascia)
serratus posterior inferior.a: Draws the lower ribs downward and backward (assists forced expiration; its role may also be mainly proprioceptive)
serratus posterior inferior.c: Lies deep to latissimus dorsi, and its respiratory function remains debated; it may be tender when there is aching at the thoracolumbar junction.

serratus posterior superior.kid: A thin, saw-toothed muscle in your upper back that helps lift your upper ribs when you breathe in.
serratus posterior superior.o: Lower part of the ligamentum nuchae; spinous processes of C7–T3
serratus posterior superior.i: Upper borders of ribs 2–5 (lateral to the angles of the ribs)
serratus posterior superior.a: Elevates ribs 2–5 (assists inspiration; its role may also be mainly proprioceptive)
serratus posterior superior.c: Lies deep to the rhomboids; its tender points are covered by the scapula, so the scapula must be protracted before they can be reached easily.

set of anterior cervical intertransversa.kid: Little muscles joining the sides of each bone in your neck that help your neck bend sideways and stay steady.
set of anterior cervical intertransversa.o: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae
set of anterior cervical intertransversa.i: Anterior tubercle of the transverse process of the cervical vertebra above
set of anterior cervical intertransversa.a: Ipsilateral lateral flexion of the cervical spine; segmental stability and proprioception
set of anterior cervical intertransversa.n: Anterior rami of the cervical nerves
set of anterior cervical intertransversa.c: The anterior rami of the cervical nerves pass between them and the posterior intertransversarii; with a high density of muscle spindles, they mainly serve position sense of the cervical spine.

set of dorsal interossei of foot.kid: Four little muscles between the bones of your foot that help you spread your toes out like a fan.
set of dorsal interossei of foot.o: Facing surfaces of two adjacent metatarsals (four muscles, all bipennate)
set of dorsal interossei of foot.i: Bases of the proximal phalanges and the extensor expansions (1st to the medial side of the 2nd toe; 2nd–4th to the lateral sides of toes 2–4)
set of dorsal interossei of foot.a: Abduction of toes 2–4 (about the 2nd toe as the axis); flex the metatarsophalangeal joints and assist extension of the interphalangeal joints
set of dorsal interossei of foot.n: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
set of dorsal interossei of foot.b: Arcuate artery; dorsal and plantar metatarsal arteries
set of dorsal interossei of foot.c: Part of the fourth layer of plantar muscles; weakness reduces forefoot stability and predisposes to claw toes, and they can be trained with toe-spreading exercises.

set of dorsal interossei of hand.kid: Four little muscles between the bones of your hand that help you spread your fingers out wide.
set of dorsal interossei of hand.o: Facing surfaces of two adjacent metacarpals (four muscles, all bipennate)
set of dorsal interossei of hand.i: Bases of the proximal phalanges of digits 2–4 and the extensor expansions (1st and 2nd to the radial sides of the index and middle fingers; 3rd and 4th to the ulnar sides of the middle and ring fingers)
set of dorsal interossei of hand.a: Finger abduction (about the middle finger as the axis); flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints
set of dorsal interossei of hand.n: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
set of dorsal interossei of hand.b: Dorsal metacarpal arteries; palmar metacarpal arteries
set of dorsal interossei of hand.c: The first dorsal interosseous lies in the first web space and is easy to palpate; its wasting and hollowing is a classic sign of ulnar neuropathy.

set of interspinales cervicis.kid: Little muscles joining the bumps on the back of each bone in your neck that help your neck tip backward and stay steady.
set of interspinales cervicis.o: Superior surfaces of the spinous processes (C3–T1)
set of interspinales cervicis.i: Inferior surface of the spinous process of the vertebra above (C2–C7)
set of interspinales cervicis.a: Assist extension of the cervical spine; segmental stability and proprioception
set of interspinales cervicis.n: Posterior rami of the cervical nerves
set of interspinales cervicis.b: Deep cervical artery; descending branch of the occipital artery
set of interspinales cervicis.c: Arranged in pairs on either side of the interspinous ligaments, about 6 pairs in all; best developed in the cervical spine.

set of interspinales lumborum.kid: These are tiny muscles between the bony bumps of your lower back that help you stand up straight and keep each back bone steady.
set of interspinales lumborum.o: Superior border of the spinous process of the vertebra below (between adjacent spinous processes L1–L5, paired left and right)
set of interspinales lumborum.i: Inferior border of the spinous process of the lumbar vertebra above
set of interspinales lumborum.a: Assist lumbar extension; segmental stabilization and proprioceptive feedback
set of interspinales lumborum.n: Posterior rami of lumbar spinal nerves (L1–L5)
set of interspinales lumborum.b: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries
set of interspinales lumborum.c: Short, small muscles with a high muscle spindle density; their main role is segmental stability and position sense, and they are activated together with multifidus during lumbar stabilization training.

set of interspinales thoracis.kid: These are very tiny muscles between the bony bumps of your back that help two neighboring back bones stay snug and steady.
set of interspinales thoracis.o: Superior border of the spinous process of the thoracic vertebra below (usually present only between T1–T2 and T11–T12)
set of interspinales thoracis.i: Inferior border of the spinous process of the thoracic vertebra above
set of interspinales thoracis.a: Assist thoracic extension; segmental stabilization and proprioception
set of interspinales thoracis.n: Posterior rami of thoracic spinal nerves
set of interspinales thoracis.b: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
set of interspinales thoracis.c: The thoracic interspinales are often poorly developed or absent, and are distinct only at the uppermost and lowermost thoracic segments.

set of lateral lumbar intertransversariu.kid: These muscles join the bony bumps on the sides of your lower back bones, helping you bend sideways and keeping your lower back steady.
set of lateral lumbar intertransversariu.o: Superior border of the transverse (costal) process of the lumbar vertebra below
set of lateral lumbar intertransversariu.i: Inferior border of the transverse (costal) process of the lumbar vertebra above
set of lateral lumbar intertransversariu.a: Assist ipsilateral lateral flexion of the lumbar spine; bilateral contraction stabilizes the lumbar segments
set of lateral lumbar intertransversariu.n: Anterior rami of lumbar spinal nerves (L1–L4)
set of lateral lumbar intertransversariu.c: Unlike the medial intertransversarii, the lateral ones are supplied by anterior rami of the spinal nerves and developmentally belong to the ventrolateral trunk musculature.

set of levatores costarum breves.kid: These muscles run from your back bones down to the rib just below, and help lift your ribs when you breathe in.
set of levatores costarum breves.o: Tips of the transverse processes of C7–T11
set of levatores costarum breves.i: Outer surface of the rib immediately below (between the tubercle and the angle of the rib)
set of levatores costarum breves.a: Elevate the ribs, assisting inspiration; assist thoracic extension, lateral flexion and rotation
set of levatores costarum breves.b: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
set of levatores costarum breves.c: Lie deep to erector spinae near the costotransverse joints; local tenderness here is common with costovertebral joint dysfunction.

set of levatores costarum longi.kid: These muscles run down from your back bones, skip over one rib and grab the next one down to help you breathe in.
set of levatores costarum longi.o: Tips of the transverse processes of the lower thoracic vertebrae (about T7–T10)
set of levatores costarum longi.i: Pass down over one rib to insert on the outer surface of the second rib below (between the tubercle and the angle of the rib)
set of levatores costarum longi.a: Elevate the ribs, assisting inspiration; assist thoracic extension, lateral flexion and rotation
set of levatores costarum longi.n: Posterior rami of spinal nerves (lower thoracic nerves)
set of levatores costarum longi.b: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
set of levatores costarum longi.c: Found only in the lower thoracic region; their fibers are longer than those of the levatores costarum breves and span two intercostal spaces.

set of lumbricals of hand.kid: Four little worm-shaped muscles in your palm that bend your fingers at the bottom while keeping the rest straight, so you can pinch things.
set of lumbricals of hand.o: Tendons of flexor digitorum profundus (1st and 2nd from the radial side of a single tendon; 3rd and 4th from two adjacent tendons)
set of lumbricals of hand.i: Radial side of the extensor expansion (dorsal digital expansion) of digits 2–5
set of lumbricals of hand.a: Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints
set of lumbricals of hand.n: 1st and 2nd lumbricals: median nerve; 3rd and 4th lumbricals: deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
set of lumbricals of hand.b: Superficial and deep palmar arches, common palmar digital arteries
set of lumbricals of hand.c: Neither the origin nor the insertion is on bone; the "lumbrical grip" (metacarpophalangeal flexion with interphalangeal extension) is a common position for training the intrinsic hand muscles.

set of medial lumbar intertransversarius.kid: These are tiny muscles at the back of your lower back bones that link one bone to the next and help your lower back stay steady.
set of medial lumbar intertransversarius.o: Accessory process of the lumbar vertebra above
set of medial lumbar intertransversarius.i: Mammillary process of the lumbar vertebra below
set of medial lumbar intertransversarius.a: Segmental stabilization and proprioception; assist ipsilateral lateral flexion of the lumbar spine
set of medial lumbar intertransversarius.n: Posterior rami of lumbar spinal nerves (L1–L4)
set of medial lumbar intertransversarius.b: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries
set of medial lumbar intertransversarius.c: Supplied by posterior rami of the spinal nerves, so they are true intrinsic back muscles; with a high muscle spindle density, they are regarded as position sensors of the spine.

set of palmar interossei of hand.kid: Muscles hidden between the bones of your palm that pull your spread fingers back toward the middle finger, like closing a fan.
set of palmar interossei of hand.o: Ulnar side of the 2nd metacarpal, radial sides of the 4th and 5th metacarpals (palmar aspect)
set of palmar interossei of hand.i: Base of the proximal phalanx and extensor expansion of the same finger (ulnar side of digit 2; radial side of digits 4 and 5)
set of palmar interossei of hand.a: Adduct the fingers (toward the middle finger); assist metacarpophalangeal flexion and interphalangeal extension
set of palmar interossei of hand.n: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1)
set of palmar interossei of hand.b: Palmar metacarpal arteries from the deep palmar arch
set of palmar interossei of hand.c: Mnemonic PAD (Palmar ADduct); the paper-grip test between the fingers checks ulnar nerve function, and adduction is weak with ulnar nerve injury.

set of posterior cervical intertransvers.kid: Tiny muscles between the bony bumps on the sides of your neck that help tilt your head sideways and keep your neck steady.
set of posterior cervical intertransvers.o: Posterior tubercle of the transverse process of the cervical vertebra below
set of posterior cervical intertransvers.i: Posterior tubercle of the transverse process of the cervical vertebra above
set of posterior cervical intertransvers.a: Assist ipsilateral lateral flexion of the cervical spine; stabilize the cervical segments
set of posterior cervical intertransvers.n: Anterior rami (lateral part) and posterior rami (medial part) of cervical spinal nerves
set of posterior cervical intertransvers.b: Branches of the vertebral, deep cervical and occipital arteries
set of posterior cervical intertransvers.c: The anterior rami of the cervical spinal nerves emerge between the anterior and posterior intertransversarii, an anatomical landmark for identifying the cervical nerve roots.

short head of biceps brachii.kid: The inner half of the muscle that bulges on the front of your upper arm, helping you bend your elbow and turn your palm up.
short head of biceps brachii.o: Tip of the coracoid process of the scapula (common origin with coracobrachialis)
short head of biceps brachii.i: Radial tuberosity; also to the antebrachial fascia via the bicipital aponeurosis
short head of biceps brachii.a: Elbow flexion, forearm supination; assists shoulder flexion and adduction
short head of biceps brachii.b: Muscular branches of the brachial artery
short head of biceps brachii.c: Shares the coracoid process attachment with coracobrachialis and pectoralis minor, so tenderness at the coracoid must be differentiated among them; supination strength is greatest with the elbow flexed to 90°.

short head of biceps femoris.kid: A deeper muscle on the outer back of your thigh that helps you bend your knee and turn your lower leg outward.
short head of biceps femoris.o: Lateral lip of the linea aspera, lateral supracondylar line and lateral intermuscular septum of the femur
short head of biceps femoris.i: Head of the fibula (common tendon with the long head)
short head of biceps femoris.a: Knee flexion; laterally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed
short head of biceps femoris.n: Common fibular division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
short head of biceps femoris.b: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery, muscular branches of the popliteal artery
short head of biceps femoris.c: The only part of the hamstrings that does not cross the hip joint and is supplied by the common fibular division, so it takes no part in hip extension.

soleus.kid: A flat muscle hidden inside your calf that helps you stand on tiptoe and stops you from tipping forward when you stand.
soleus.o: Head and upper 1/3 of the posterior surface of the fibular shaft, soleal line and middle 1/3 of the medial border of the tibia, and the tendinous arch between them
soleus.i: Posterior surface of the calcaneal tuberosity via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
soleus.a: Ankle plantarflexion; stabilizes the leg in standing and prevents the body from leaning forward
soleus.b: Posterior tibial artery, fibular artery, sural branches of the popliteal artery
soleus.c: Does not cross the knee, so it can be stretched in isolation by ankle dorsiflexion with the knee flexed; known as the "second heart" because its contraction aids venous return from the lower limb.

spinal part of deltoid.kid: The muscle at the back of your shoulder that helps you pull your arm backward, like rowing a boat or pulling open a drawer.
spinal part of deltoid.o: Inferior border of the spine of the scapula
spinal part of deltoid.i: Deltoid tuberosity on the lateral shaft of the humerus
spinal part of deltoid.a: Shoulder extension, lateral rotation, horizontal abduction
spinal part of deltoid.b: Posterior circumflex humeral artery, deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial artery
spinal part of deltoid.c: The posterior fibers are often weak in people with rounded shoulders; prone horizontal abduction or reverse flyes train them specifically.

spinalis cervicis.kid: A thin, long muscle right beside the middle bones at the back of your neck that helps you tip your neck back and lift your head.
spinalis cervicis.o: Lower part of the ligamentum nuchae, spinous process of C7 (sometimes T1–T2)
spinalis cervicis.i: Spinous process of the axis (C2), sometimes extending to the spinous processes of C3–C4
spinalis cervicis.n: Posterior rami of cervical spinal nerves
spinalis cervicis.b: Deep cervical artery, muscular branches of the vertebral artery
spinalis cervicis.c: The cervical part of the most medial column of erector spinae; often poorly developed or absent and highly variable.

spinalis thoracis.kid: A thin, long muscle hugging both sides of the middle of your backbone that helps you keep your back straight and not slouch.
spinalis thoracis.i: Spinous processes of the upper thoracic vertebrae (about T2–T8)
spinalis thoracis.a: Thoracic extension; unilateral contraction assists lateral flexion
spinalis thoracis.n: Posterior rami of thoracic spinal nerves
spinalis thoracis.b: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
spinalis thoracis.c: The most medial and smallest of the three erector spinae columns, closely blended with longissimus thoracis and hard to separate from it.

splenius capitis.kid: A muscle wrapped slantwise around the back of your neck like a bandage that helps you lift your head back and turn it.
splenius capitis.o: Lower half of the ligamentum nuchae, spinous processes of C7–T3 (T4)
splenius capitis.i: Mastoid process of the temporal bone, lateral 1/3 of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone
splenius capitis.a: Bilateral: extension of the head and neck; unilateral: ipsilateral rotation and lateral flexion of the head and neck
splenius capitis.n: Lateral branches of the posterior rami of the middle cervical spinal nerves (C2–C4)
splenius capitis.b: Muscular branches of the occipital artery, deep cervical artery
splenius capitis.c: Commonly tight with forward head posture and acute stiff neck, and its trigger points can refer pain to the top of the head; palpable between trapezius and sternocleidomastoid.

splenius cervicis.kid: A muscle running slantwise from your upper back to the top part of your neck that helps you stretch your neck back and turn it.
splenius cervicis.i: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1–C3
splenius cervicis.a: Bilateral: cervical extension; unilateral: ipsilateral rotation and lateral flexion of the cervical spine
splenius cervicis.n: Lateral branches of the posterior rami of the lower cervical spinal nerves (C5–C7)
splenius cervicis.b: Branches of the occipital, deep cervical and transverse cervical arteries
splenius cervicis.c: Inserts on the upper cervical transverse processes together with levator scapulae, and the two are often tight together when neck rotation is restricted.

sternocleidomastoid.kid: The big slanted muscle on each side of your neck that pops out when you turn your head, helping you turn, nod and tilt your head.
sternocleidomastoid.o: Sternal head: upper anterior surface of the manubrium; clavicular head: superior surface of the medial 1/3 of the clavicle
sternocleidomastoid.i: Lateral surface of the mastoid process of the temporal bone, lateral half of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone
sternocleidomastoid.a: Unilateral: lateral flexion of the head to the same side with rotation of the face to the opposite side; bilateral: neck flexion, head protraction, and assists forced inspiration
sternocleidomastoid.n: Accessory nerve (CN XI); anterior rami of C2–C3 for proprioception
sternocleidomastoid.b: Sternocleidomastoid branches of the occipital and superior thyroid arteries
sternocleidomastoid.c: The affected muscle in congenital muscular torticollis; often shortened and tight with forward head posture. It is the landmark dividing the anterior and posterior triangles of the neck.

sternocostal part of pectoralis major.kid: The lower half of your biggest chest muscle, helping you hug things, push doors and pull your raised arm back down.
sternocostal part of pectoralis major.o: Anterior surface of the sternum, costal cartilages 1–6, aponeurosis of the external oblique
sternocostal part of pectoralis major.i: Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus (crest of the greater tubercle)
sternocostal part of pectoralis major.a: Shoulder adduction, medial rotation, horizontal adduction; extends the arm downward from a flexed position
sternocostal part of pectoralis major.b: Pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery, perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery, lateral thoracic artery
sternocostal part of pectoralis major.c: Commonly shortened with rounded shoulders; the sternocostal fibers are stretched with the shoulder abducted about 120°–135° and horizontally abducted. Tendon ruptures during the bench press mostly occur in this part.

sternohyoid.kid: A thin, long strap muscle at the front of your neck that pulls the little bone above your throat back down after you swallow.
sternohyoid.o: Posterior surface of the manubrium, posterior surface of the medial end of the clavicle and the posterior sternoclavicular ligament
sternohyoid.i: Inferior border of the body of the hyoid bone
sternohyoid.a: Depresses the hyoid (returning it after swallowing, phonation); fixes the hyoid so the suprahyoid muscles can open the mouth
sternohyoid.b: Branches of the superior thyroid and lingual arteries
sternohyoid.c: One of the infrahyoid (strap) muscles; swallowing and voice may be affected after a whiplash injury of the neck or thyroid surgery.

sternothyroid.kid: A deeper strap muscle at the front of your neck that pulls your voice box down after you swallow or when you make low sounds.
sternothyroid.o: Posterior surface of the manubrium, 1st costal cartilage
sternothyroid.i: Oblique line of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage
sternothyroid.b: Branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries
sternothyroid.c: Lies deep to sternohyoid and covers the front of the thyroid gland; it is stretched out when the thyroid enlarges.

stylohyoid.kid: A thin muscle running from a little pointy bone under your ear to the small bone above your throat, pulling it up and back when you swallow.
stylohyoid.o: Posterolateral surface of the styloid process of the temporal bone
stylohyoid.i: Junction of the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone
stylohyoid.a: Elevates and retracts the hyoid (elongating the floor of the mouth during swallowing)
stylohyoid.n: Stylohyoid branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
stylohyoid.b: Branches of the facial, occipital and posterior auricular arteries
stylohyoid.c: Its tendon splits near the insertion to let the intermediate tendon of the digastric pass through; an elongated styloid process (Eagle syndrome) can cause throat pain on swallowing.

subclavius.kid: A small muscle hiding under your collarbone that holds the collarbone down in place and protects the blood vessels and nerves underneath.
subclavius.o: Junction of the 1st rib and its costal cartilage
subclavius.i: Subclavian groove on the inferior surface of the middle 1/3 of the clavicle
subclavius.a: Depresses and draws the clavicle forward; stabilizes the sternoclavicular joint
subclavius.b: Clavicular branch of the thoracoacromial artery
subclavius.c: Cushions and protects the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus in clavicle fractures; when tight it may contribute to narrowing of the costoclavicular space (thoracic outlet syndrome).

subscapularis.kid: A muscle hidden on the front of your shoulder blade against your ribs that helps turn your arm inward and hugs your shoulder joint tight.
subscapularis.i: Lesser tubercle of the humerus and the anterior part of the shoulder joint capsule
subscapularis.a: Medial rotation of the shoulder; stabilizes the humeral head in the glenoid and prevents anterior dislocation
subscapularis.b: Subscapular artery, suprascapular artery, circumflex scapular artery
subscapularis.c: The largest rotator cuff muscle and its only medial rotator; tested with the lift-off test and the belly-press test. Can be palpated from the anterior border of the axilla toward the anterior surface of the scapula.

superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.kid: One of the muscles in the fleshy pad at the bottom of your thumb that helps you bend your thumb toward your palm to grab things.
superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.o: Flexor retinaculum, tubercle of the trapezium
superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.i: Radial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb (via the radial sesamoid)
superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.a: Flexes the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb; assists thumb opposition
superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.n: Recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8–T1)
superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.b: Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.c: A thenar muscle that wastes along with the rest of the thenar eminence in long-standing carpal tunnel syndrome; the flexor pollicis longus tendon runs between the superficial and deep heads.

superficial part of masseter.kid: The muscle at the back of your cheek that bulges when you clench your teeth, helping you close your mouth hard to bite.
superficial part of masseter.o: Maxillary process of the zygomatic bone, anterior 2/3 of the inferior border of the zygomatic arch
superficial part of masseter.i: Angle of the mandible and the lower half of the lateral surface of the ramus (masseteric tuberosity)
superficial part of masseter.a: Elevates the mandible (closing the jaw to bite); assists mandibular protrusion
superficial part of masseter.n: Masseteric nerve from the mandibular nerve (CN V3)
superficial part of masseter.b: Masseteric branch of the maxillary artery, transverse facial artery, facial artery
superficial part of masseter.c: Easily palpated above the angle of the mandible when the teeth are clenched; with bruxism and temporomandibular disorders it is often hypertrophied, with trigger points that refer toothache or preauricular pain.

superior oblique part of longus colli.kid: A very deep muscle right on the front of your neck bones that helps you nod and tuck your chin so your neck doesn't wobble.
superior oblique part of longus colli.o: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3–C5
superior oblique part of longus colli.i: Anterior tubercle on the anterior arch of the atlas (C1)
superior oblique part of longus colli.a: Flexes the cervical spine; unilateral contraction assists ipsilateral lateral flexion and rotation; stabilizes the cervical spine
superior oblique part of longus colli.n: Anterior rami of cervical spinal nerves (C2–C6)
superior oblique part of longus colli.b: Branches of the ascending pharyngeal, ascending cervical and vertebral arteries
superior oblique part of longus colli.c: One of the deep neck flexors; often inhibited after neck pain and whiplash injury, and reactivated with craniocervical flexion (chin-tuck) training.

supinator.kid: A muscle wrapped around the bone just below your elbow that helps you turn your palm up, like turning a doorknob or a screw.
supinator.o: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus, radial collateral ligament, annular ligament of the radius, supinator crest of the ulna
supinator.i: Lateral, anterior and posterior surfaces of the proximal 1/3 of the radius
supinator.a: Forearm supination (acts at any elbow angle)
supinator.n: Deep branch of the radial nerve (C6–C7)
supinator.b: Radial recurrent artery, posterior interosseous artery, interosseous recurrent artery
supinator.c: The deep branch of the radial nerve passes between its superficial and deep layers (arcade of Frohse); entrapment here causes posterior interosseous nerve syndrome, which must be differentiated from tennis elbow.

supraspinatus.kid: A muscle tucked in the hollow on top of your shoulder blade that helps you start lifting your arm out to the side.
supraspinatus.i: Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus and the superior part of the shoulder joint capsule
supraspinatus.a: Initiates shoulder abduction and assists the deltoid in abduction; holds the humeral head steady in the glenoid
supraspinatus.c: The most commonly torn rotator cuff tendon, prone to impingement as it passes through the subacromial space; tested with the empty can test and the drop arm test.

temporalis.kid: The fan-shaped muscle at your temples on the sides of your head that moves when you chew and helps you close your mouth.
temporalis.o: Temporal fossa (frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones below the inferior temporal line) and the deep surface of the temporal fascia
temporalis.i: Tip and medial surface of the coronoid process of the mandible, anterior border of the ramus of the mandible
temporalis.a: Elevates the mandible (closes the jaw); posterior fibers retract the mandible; unilaterally assists side-to-side grinding
temporalis.n: Deep temporal nerves from the mandibular nerve (CN V3)
temporalis.b: Deep temporal arteries from the maxillary artery, middle temporal artery from the superficial temporal artery
temporalis.c: Its contraction can be felt at the temple when clenching the teeth; tightness or trigger points commonly cause tension-type headache in the temporal region and pain in the upper teeth.

temporoparietalis.kid: A thin sheet of muscle above your ear that can tighten your scalp, and some people can even use it to wiggle their ears.
temporoparietalis.i: Lateral border of the epicranial aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica)
temporoparietalis.a: Tightens the scalp, elevates the auricle
temporoparietalis.n: Temporal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
temporoparietalis.c: Part of the epicranius; thin and variable, and of little functional importance.

tendinous arch of levator ani.kid: A strong band inside your hips that gives the muscles holding up the organs in your tummy a place to hang on to.
tendinous arch of levator ani.o: Posterior surface of the body of the pubis
tendinous arch of levator ani.a: Thickened band of the obturator internus fascia that gives origin to levator ani (iliococcygeus) and supports the pelvic floor
tendinous arch of levator ani.c: When its attachment becomes lax or torn through childbirth or aging, pelvic floor support is inadequate, and pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence may develop.

tensor fasciae latae.kid: A small muscle at the front of the outside of your hip that tightens the long band down the outside of your thigh, helping you lift your leg and stand steady.
tensor fasciae latae.o: Anterior superior iliac spine, anterior part of the outer lip of the iliac crest
tensor fasciae latae.i: Iliotibial tract (through it to Gerdy's tubercle on the lateral condyle of the tibia)
tensor fasciae latae.a: Hip flexion, abduction, medial rotation; helps stabilize the extended knee via the iliotibial tract
tensor fasciae latae.b: Superior gluteal artery, ascending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery
tensor fasciae latae.c: Often overused in compensation when gluteus medius is weak; tightness is associated with iliotibial band syndrome (runner's knee) and is assessed with the Ober test.

teres major.kid: A round muscle from the bottom corner of your shoulder blade to your arm that helps pull your arm down and back and turn it inward.
teres major.o: Dorsal surface of the inferior angle of the scapula
teres major.i: Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus (crest of the lesser tubercle)
teres major.c: Known as "lat's little helper", it forms the posterior axillary fold together with latissimus dorsi; tightness limits shoulder flexion and lateral rotation. It is not part of the rotator cuff.

teres minor.kid: A small muscle on the outer edge of your shoulder blade that helps turn your arm outward and keeps your shoulder joint steady.
teres minor.o: Dorsal surface of the upper 2/3 of the lateral border of the scapula
teres minor.i: Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus and the posterior part of the shoulder joint capsule
teres minor.a: Lateral rotation of the shoulder; stabilizes the humeral head; weak adduction
teres minor.b: Circumflex scapular artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery
teres minor.c: One of the rotator cuff muscles; tested with the hornblower's sign. It may atrophy in isolation when the axillary nerve is compressed in quadrilateral space syndrome.
